questions.title: recommended replacement for FastAPI().extra dropped in v0.145.0
questions.question:
### First Check

- [X] I added a very descriptive title here.
- [X] I used the GitHub search to find a similar question and didn't find it.
- [X] I searched the FastAPI documentation, with the integrated search.

- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Swagger UI](https://github.com/swagger-api/swagger-ui).
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [ReDoc](https://github.com/Redocly/redoc).

### Commit to Help

- [X] I commit to help with one of those options 👆

### Example Code

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.routing import iter_route_contexts
from fastapi.openapi.utils import _get_openapi_dependency_data, _get_openapi_security_definitions, _get_api_route_for_openapi
from fastapi.openapi.utils import get_openapi


def iter_public_routes(routes):
	'''Iterate over all public routes'''
	for route_context in iter_route_contexts(routes):
		route = _get_api_route_for_openapi(route_context)
		if route and hasattr(route, 'dependant'):
			dependency_data = _get_openapi_dependency_data(route.dependant)
			_, operation_security = _get_openapi_security_definitions(security_dependencies=dependency_data.security_dependencies)
			if not operation_security:
				yield route


app = FastAPI(title='Test', public_openapi_schema={})


@app.get("/openapi.public.json", response_model=dict[str, Any], include_in_schema=False)
def public_openapi() -> dict:
	if not app.extra.get('public_openapi_schema'):
		app.extra['public_openapi_schema'] = get_openapi(
			title=f'{app.title} [public interface]',
			description=app.description,
			version=app.version,
			routes=list(iter_public_routes(app.routes)),
		)
	return app.extra['public_openapi_schema']
```


### Description

We cached the specially filtered output of `get_openapi` to only include public endpoints in a key of `FastAPI().extra`. If I remember correctly, this behaviour was in principle copied from an example in the docs some time ago and follows the advice given here (e.g. https://github.com/fastapi/fastapi/discussions/15784#discussioncomment-17385817).

Since v0.145.0 dropped the `extra`, is there a recommended alternative way or should such caches be stored "outside" the app (e.g. using functools)?

### Operating System

Linux

### Operating System Details

Ubuntu 24.04 LTS

### FastAPI Version

fastapi==0.143.0

### Pydantic Version

pydantic==2.14.1

### Python Version

Python 3.15.0

### Additional Context

_No response_
questions.answer:
Use `app.state.public_openapi_schema` for this cache; you don't need to move it outside the app or use `functools`. [#16518](https://github.com/fastapi/fastapi/pull/16518) removed the unused `**extra` kwargs from `FastAPI()`, but FastAPI 0.149.0 still [initializes `app.state` as an application-wide `State` object](https://github.com/fastapi/fastapi/blob/4001c90dad1924b6d10624c7523d7264f4bf9f97/fastapi/applications.py#L947-L963).

Keep your `iter_public_routes()` and imports, add `from typing import Any`, and replace the app initialization and endpoint with:

```python
app = FastAPI(title='Test')
app.state.public_openapi_schema = None


@app.get('/openapi.public.json', response_model=dict[str, Any], include_in_schema=False)
def public_openapi() -> dict:
    if app.state.public_openapi_schema is None:
        app.state.public_openapi_schema = get_openapi(
            title=f'{app.title} [public interface]',
            description=app.description,
            version=app.version,
            routes=list(iter_public_routes(app.routes)),
        )
    return app.state.public_openapi_schema

```

I ran this with your route-filtering function on FastAPI 0.149.0, Python 3.12.3/Linux, with one public route and one `APIKeyHeader`-secured route:

```text
same cached object: True
public schema paths: ['/public']
GET /openapi.public.json: 200
normal OpenAPI still contains /private: True
```

I didn't run Python 3.15 or your full application. To confirm the migration, check that `/openapi.public.json` returns your filtered schema and `/openapi.json` retains the regular schema.

questions.title: Support ReDoc 3 in get_redoc_html(): its bundle needs <script type="module">
questions.question:
### First Check

- [X] I added a very descriptive title here.
- [X] I used the GitHub search to find a similar question and didn't find it.
- [X] I searched the FastAPI documentation, with the integrated search.
- [X] I already searched in Google "How to X in FastAPI" and didn't find any information.
- [X] I already read and followed all the tutorial in the docs and didn't find an answer.
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Pydantic](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic).
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Swagger UI](https://github.com/swagger-api/swagger-ui).
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [ReDoc](https://github.com/Redocly/redoc).

### Commit to Help

- [X] I commit to help with one of those options 👆

### Example Code

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.openapi.docs import get_redoc_html

app = FastAPI(redoc_url=None)


@app.get("/redoc", include_in_schema=False)
def redoc():
    return get_redoc_html(
        openapi_url=app.openapi_url,
        title=f"{app.title} - ReDoc",
        redoc_js_url="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/redoc@3/bundles/redoc.standalone.js",
    )


@app.get("/items/{item_id}")
def read_item(item_id: int):
    return {"item_id": item_id}
```


### Description

I work on Redoc at Redocly. We've released ReDoc 3.0, and its standalone bundle is ES-module only: it has to be loaded with `<script type="module">`. `get_redoc_html()` always renders a classic `<script src="...">`, so passing a ReDoc 3 URL as `redoc_js_url` (example above) gives a blank `/redoc` page with this console error:

```
Cannot use 'import.meta' outside a module
```

The default URL is pinned to `redoc@2`, so nothing is broken today. This is only about being able to opt into ReDoc 3.

Simply switching the tag isn't safe: the ReDoc 2 bundle fails under `type="module"`, which would break everyone self-hosting the 2.x bundle as described in [Custom Docs UI Static Assets](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/how-to/custom-docs-ui-assets/). So it would need to be opt-in.

What I tested (FastAPI 0.143.0 in Chrome, the generated HTML with only the script tag changed):

| Bundle  | Script tag              | Result |
|---------|-------------------------|--------|
| redoc@2 | classic (today's default) | works |
| redoc@3 | classic                 | blank page, `Cannot use 'import.meta' outside a module` |
| redoc@3 | `type="module"`         | works |
| redoc@2 | `type="module"`         | blank page, `Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'null')` |

A possible shape, opt-in with the default unchanged:

```python
get_redoc_html(
    openapi_url=app.openapi_url,
    title=f"{app.title} - ReDoc",
    redoc_js_url="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/redoc@3/bundles/redoc.standalone.js",
    redoc_js_module=True,  # renders <script type="module" src="...">
)
```

I saw in #12955 that you plan to rework how ReDoc is set up, so I'm happy either to send a small PR for this now (parameter, test, a note in the docs) or to leave it for that refactor. Whatever works best for you, and happy to help with anything ReDoc-related on the FastAPI side.

### Operating System

macOS

### Operating System Details

_No response_

### FastAPI Version

0.143.0

### Pydantic Version

2.14.1

### Python Version

3.13.16

### Additional Context

_No response_
questions.answer:
Thanks!

I think we should wait for that rework Sebastian is planning.

Let's document here a workaround people can use now:

```py
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.openapi.docs import get_redoc_html
from fastapi.responses import HTMLResponse

app = FastAPI(redoc_url=None)


@app.get("/redoc", include_in_schema=False)
async def redoc():
    response = get_redoc_html(
        openapi_url=app.openapi_url,
        title=f"{app.title} - ReDoc",
        redoc_js_url="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/redoc@3/bundles/redoc.standalone.js",
    )
    html = response.body.decode("utf-8")
    html = html.replace("<script src=", '<script type="module" src=', 1)

    return HTMLResponse(html)


@app.get("/items/{item_id}")
async def read_item(item_id: int):
    return {"item_id": item_id}
```

questions.title: Telemetry: supported way to turn off automatic OTLP export for a whole process when another library already exports
questions.question:
### First Check

- [X] I added a very descriptive title here.
- [X] I used the GitHub search to find a similar question and didn't find it.
- [X] I searched the FastAPI documentation, with the integrated search.
- [X] I already searched in Google "How to X in FastAPI" and didn't find any information.
- [X] I already read and followed all the tutorial in the docs and didn't find an answer.
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Pydantic](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic).
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Swagger UI](https://github.com/swagger-api/swagger-ui).
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [ReDoc](https://github.com/Redocly/redoc).

### Commit to Help

- [X] I commit to help with one of those options 👆

### Example Code

```python
import os

from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient
from opentelemetry import metrics, trace
from opentelemetry.sdk.metrics import MeterProvider
from opentelemetry.sdk.metrics.export import ConsoleMetricExporter, PeriodicExportingMetricReader
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace import TracerProvider
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace.export import BatchSpanProcessor, ConsoleSpanExporter

# Another library has already configured providers with its own exporters.
devnull = open(os.devnull, "w")
tracer_provider = TracerProvider()
tracer_provider.add_span_processor(BatchSpanProcessor(ConsoleSpanExporter(out=devnull)))
trace.set_tracer_provider(tracer_provider)
meter_provider = MeterProvider(metric_readers=[PeriodicExportingMetricReader(ConsoleMetricExporter(out=devnull))])
metrics.set_meter_provider(meter_provider)

with TestClient(FastAPI()):
    pass

print(
    "span processors:", len(tracer_provider._active_span_processor._span_processors),
    "metric readers:", len(meter_provider._all_metric_readers),
)
```

Run with `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT=http://localhost:4318`, then again with `OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER=none OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER=none OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER=none` added:

```
OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT set                   -> span processors: 2 metric readers: 2
... plus OTEL_{TRACES,METRICS,LOGS}_EXPORTER=none -> span processors: 1 metric readers: 1
```

### Description

**What I'm trying to achieve.** We run several FastAPI servers per job ([NeMo Gym](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Gym)). In each process, a telemetry library ([nemo-lens](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Lens)) creates the OpenTelemetry tracer, meter and logger providers and adds its own OTLP exporters to them. That library finds the collector through `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT`, so the variable is set in every process.

Since 0.142.0, FastAPI sees the same variable at startup and adds a second exporter to those providers. The docs say this is intended ("Existing exporters continue sending data to their destinations"). For us it means every span is exported twice, and each metric is exported by two readers with separate state. The cumulative histogram `_sum` series then dips slightly from time to time, Prometheus treats each dip as a counter reset, and `rate()` and `increase()` on those series give values that are far too large.

We'd like a way to say, once per process, that export is already handled and FastAPI should not add its own exporters, without touching every `FastAPI()` call.

**Why `telemetry={"auto_configure": False}` doesn't fully cover it.** It works, but only for apps whose constructor we control and remember to change:

- Apps are built in many places: base server classes, plugins that third parties contribute, and helper scripts. One forgotten `FastAPI()` silently brings the duplicates back.
- Some FastAPI apps in the same environment come from other libraries, so we can't change their constructors.

The part of the stack that knows export is already handled is the telemetry library, which owns the providers. It doesn't create the apps, though.

**What already seems to work.** Setting `OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER`, `OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER` and `OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER` to `none` makes `_export_endpoint` return `None`, so FastAPI adds nothing (see the output above). `test_no_implicit_export` in `tests/test_telemetry/test_runtime.py` covers this. Our telemetry library builds its exporters explicitly and doesn't read these variables, so they would act as a process-wide "export is handled" signal.

**Questions.**

1. Is `OTEL_<SIGNAL>_EXPORTER=none` a supported way to turn off automatic export for a whole process? If so, could the "Configure providers and exporters" section of the OpenTelemetry docs say so next to the `auto_configure` example? I'm happy to open a docs PR.
2. If you'd rather not commit to that, is there another supported way for a library that owns the providers to opt every app in the process out, without access to the app constructors?

### Operating System

Linux

### Operating System Details

_No response_

### FastAPI Version

0.142.4

### Pydantic Version

2.13.5

### Python Version

3.13.14

### Additional Context

OpenTelemetry SDK 1.45.1.
questions.answer:
Thank you for the report and the clear explanation @ananthsub ! :raised_hands: 

I fixed/refactored it here: https://github.com/fastapi/fastapi/pull/16476

Now exporters are not automatically configured. So, it is opt-in, not opt-out. It can be enabled with the config `auto_configure` or with the env var `FASTAPI_OTEL_AUTO_CONFIGURE=true`. This is available in FastAPI 0.143.0, just released. :rocket:

questions.title: Telemetry: a request left out with exclude still records into the outer request's telemetry when nested in it
questions.question:
### First Check

- [X] I added a very descriptive title here.
- [X] I used the GitHub search to find a similar question and didn't find it.
- [X] I searched the FastAPI documentation, with the integrated search.
- [X] I already searched in Google "How to X in FastAPI" and didn't find any information.
- [X] I already read and followed all the tutorial in the docs and didn't find an answer.
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Pydantic](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic).
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Swagger UI](https://github.com/swagger-api/swagger-ui).
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [ReDoc](https://github.com/Redocly/redoc).

### Commit to Help

- [X] I commit to help with one of those options 👆

### Example Code

```python
import asyncio
import sys

import fastapi
import httpx
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.telemetry import get_telemetry_data
from opentelemetry import _logs, metrics, trace
from opentelemetry.sdk._logs import LoggerProvider
from opentelemetry.sdk._logs.export import InMemoryLogRecordExporter, SimpleLogRecordProcessor
from opentelemetry.sdk.metrics import MeterProvider
from opentelemetry.sdk.metrics.export import InMemoryMetricReader
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace import TracerProvider
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace.export import SimpleSpanProcessor
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace.export.in_memory_span_exporter import InMemorySpanExporter

spans = InMemorySpanExporter()
tracer_provider = TracerProvider()
tracer_provider.add_span_processor(SimpleSpanProcessor(spans))
trace.set_tracer_provider(tracer_provider)
reader = InMemoryMetricReader()
metrics.set_meter_provider(MeterProvider(metric_readers=[reader]))
logs = InMemoryLogRecordExporter()
logger_provider = LoggerProvider()
logger_provider.add_log_record_processor(SimpleLogRecordProcessor(logs))
_logs.set_logger_provider(logger_provider)


def is_internal(scope) -> bool:
    # httpx's ASGITransport puts the base URL's host into scope["server"]
    return (scope.get("server") or (None,))[0] == "internal.local"


app = FastAPI(telemetry={"auto_configure": False, "exclude": is_internal})
# an in-process client to the same app, e.g. an MCP server or a BFF calling its own API
internal = httpx.AsyncClient(transport=httpx.ASGITransport(app=app), base_url="http://internal.local")


@app.get("/inner")
def inner(n: int) -> dict:
    return {"n": n}


@app.get("/outer")
async def outer(n: str) -> dict:
    response = await internal.get("/inner", params={"n": n})
    data = get_telemetry_data()
    return {"inner_status": response.status_code, "outer_request_url": str(data.request.url)}


async def main() -> None:
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(transport=httpx.ASGITransport(app=app), base_url="http://testserver") as client:
        print("/outer?n=1  ->", (await client.get("/outer", params={"n": "1"})).json())
        print("/outer?n=x  ->", (await client.get("/outer", params={"n": "x"})).json())


asyncio.run(main())

print(f"\nfastapi {fastapi.__version__}, Python {sys.version.split()[0]}")
print("\nspans (name, parent span name):")
by_id = {span.context.span_id: span.name for span in spans.get_finished_spans()}
for span in spans.get_finished_spans():
    print(f"  {span.name:24} parent={by_id.get(span.parent.span_id) if span.parent else None}")
print("\nhttp.server.request.duration by route:")
for resource in reader.get_metrics_data().resource_metrics:
    for scope in resource.scope_metrics:
        for metric in scope.metrics:
            if metric.name == "http.server.request.duration":
                for point in metric.data.data_points:
                    print(f"  {point.attributes.get('http.route')}: {point.count}")
print("\nlog records:")
for record in logs.get_finished_logs():
    log = record.log_record
    print(f"  {log.event_name}: {log.body!r} attributes={dict(log.attributes or {})}")
```


### Description

I call my own FastAPI app in-process (an MCP server calling its REST API through `httpx.ASGITransport`) and leave those inner requests out of the native telemetry with `telemetry={"exclude": ...}`. The inner request then gets no server span and no duration metric, as expected. But because it runs inside the outer request's OpenTelemetry context, three things still land on the outer request:

- its operation spans (`fastapi.dependencies`, `fastapi.endpoint`, `fastapi.serialization`) are recorded under the outer request's span;
- its request data overwrites the outer request's `TelemetryData`: `get_telemetry_data()` in `/outer` returns the inner request's URL;
- its validation failure is logged as `fastapi.validation.failed` with `http.route=/outer`, although `/outer` was valid.

Output of the example:

```
/outer?n=1  -> {'inner_status': 200, 'outer_request_url': 'http://internal.local/inner?n=1'}
/outer?n=x  -> {'inner_status': 422, 'outer_request_url': 'http://internal.local/inner?n=x'}

fastapi 0.142.2, Python 3.13.3

spans (name, parent span name):
  fastapi.dependencies     parent=GET /outer
  fastapi.dependencies     parent=fastapi.endpoint
  fastapi.endpoint         parent=fastapi.endpoint
  fastapi.serialization    parent=fastapi.endpoint
  fastapi.endpoint         parent=GET /outer
  fastapi.serialization    parent=GET /outer
  GET /outer               parent=None
  fastapi.dependencies     parent=GET /outer
  fastapi.dependencies     parent=fastapi.endpoint
  fastapi.endpoint         parent=GET /outer
  fastapi.serialization    parent=GET /outer
  GET /outer               parent=None

http.server.request.duration by route:
  /outer: 2

log records:
  fastapi.validation.failed: 'Request validation failed' attributes={'fastapi.validation.error_count': 1, 'http.route': '/outer'}
```

I expected an excluded request to be invisible to fastapi's telemetry, including these context-based lookups, while the current span stays in place so other instrumentation still nests under the outer span. If inheriting is intended, it would help to document that `exclude` only covers the server span, the metrics and the exception log.

### Versions

fastapi 0.142.2, opentelemetry-sdk 1.45.0, httpx 0.28.1, Python 3.13.3

Run: `uv run --no-project --with "fastapi>=0.142" --with httpx --with opentelemetry-sdk python repro.py`

macOS

### Operating System Details

_No response_

### FastAPI Version

0.142.2

### Pydantic Version

2.13.5

### Python Version

3.13.3

### Additional Context

_No response_

questions.title: Native telemetry calls trace.get_tracer on every request; with the OTel SDK this re-emits every repeated warning per request
questions.question:
### First Check

- [X] I added a very descriptive title here.
- [X] I used the GitHub search to find a similar question and didn't find it.
- [X] I searched the FastAPI documentation, with the integrated search.
- [X] I already searched in Google "How to X in FastAPI" and didn't find any information.
- [X] I already read and followed all the tutorial in the docs and didn't find an answer.
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Pydantic](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic).
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Swagger UI](https://github.com/swagger-api/swagger-ui).
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [ReDoc](https://github.com/Redocly/redoc).

### Commit to Help

- [X] I commit to help with one of those options 👆

### Example Code

```python
import warnings

from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient
from opentelemetry import trace
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace import TracerProvider

trace.set_tracer_provider(TracerProvider())

app = FastAPI()


@app.get("/")
def root() -> dict[str, str]:
    warnings.warn("should be shown once per process", UserWarning)
    return {"ok": "yes"}


with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught:
    warnings.simplefilter("default")
    client = TestClient(app)
    for _ in range(5):
        client.get("/")

print(len(caught))  # prints 5; expected 1
```

### Description

With native telemetry on (the default) and the OpenTelemetry SDK's `TracerProvider` installed, every repeated warning in the application is re-emitted on every request instead of once per location. The example prints `5`; without `trace.set_tracer_provider(TracerProvider())` it prints `1`.

Cause: `NativeTelemetry.__call__` in `fastapi/telemetry/_asgi.py` calls `trace.get_tracer("fastapi", __version__, config["tracer_provider"], schema_url=_SCHEMA_URL)` on every HTTP request and WebSocket connection. In opentelemetry-sdk 1.45.0, `TracerProvider.get_tracer` calls `warnings.filterwarnings(...)` on every call, before its cache lookup. Any change to the warning filters invalidates every module's `__warningregistry__`, so Python's once-per-location dedupe resets on every request. In our service, one library's version warning was printed 3,201 times in about 5 hours.

The root defect is in the OpenTelemetry SDK (mutating global warning state on a lookup). But resolving the tracer per request is avoidable on FastAPI's side, and the meter side already avoids it: `_instruments()` caches the meter instruments per provider (`if provider is not self._provider: ...`).

Suggestion: cache the tracer per provider in the same way. Keep a `(provider, tracer)` pair on the `NativeTelemetry` instance, and re-resolve only when `config["tracer_provider"] or trace.get_tracer_provider()` is a different object. The same would apply to `_logs.get_logger(...)` when logs are enabled.

Our workaround is a `TracerProvider` subclass that caches `get_tracer` per (name, version, schema_url) in front of `super().get_tracer`.

### Operating System

macOS

### Operating System Details

Also seen in production on Linux (Debian trixie containers).

### FastAPI Version

0.142.2

### Pydantic Version

2.13.5

### Python Version

3.14.5 (production: 3.14.7)

### Additional Context

opentelemetry-sdk 1.45.0 (latest on PyPI). The `filterwarnings` call in the SDK came from open-telemetry/opentelemetry-python PR #3164.

questions.title: _endpoint_context_cache keyed by id(func) can return stale context after GC
questions.question:
### Bug

`_extract_endpoint_context()` in `fastapi/routing.py` caches per-endpoint context in `_endpoint_context_cache: dict[int, EndpointContext]` keyed by `id(func)`, holding only the `ctx` dict with no reference to `func`.

After the endpoint function is garbage-collected, CPython reuses the address for a new function object, and the cache returns the old endpoint's `file`/`line`/`function`. The cache is also never cleared, so it grows unbounded.

### Repro (fastapi 0.141.1, Python 3.14.4, Linux)

```python
import gc
from fastapi.routing import _extract_endpoint_context

def endpoint_alpha():
    pass

ctx_a = _extract_endpoint_context(endpoint_alpha)
id_a = id(endpoint_alpha)
del endpoint_alpha
gc.collect()

for i in range(50000):
    g = {}
    exec(f'def endpoint_beta_{i}():\n    pass\n', g)
    fn = g[f'endpoint_beta_{i}']
    if id(fn) == id_a:
        break
    del fn, g

stale = _extract_endpoint_context(fn)
print(stale.get('function'), '| actual:', fn.__name__)
assert stale.get('function') == fn.__name__, f"STALE: {stale} vs {fn.__name__}"
```

Output on my machine:

```
endpoint_alpha | actual: endpoint_beta_0
AssertionError: STALE: {...'function': 'endpoint_alpha'...} vs endpoint_beta_0
```

(The exact `endpoint_beta_N` index varies per run; id reuse triggered on the first try here.)

### Expected / actual

- Expected: context always describes the function passed in.
- Actual: a recycled `id()` returns another endpoint's `file`/`line`/`function`, so validation-error messages and logs can point at the wrong endpoint.

### Environment

- fastapi 0.141.1 (also present on current `master`, `fastapi/routing.py:275-297`)
- Python 3.14.4, Linux

### Possible fix direction

Validate the hit against func identity instead of trusting the bare `id()` — e.g. store `(func, ctx)` and compare with `is`, key the cache by the function object itself (or a weak reference), or drop the hand-rolled dict for a bounded cache. Related PR #16387 fixes the shared-mutation half with `.copy()` but leaves this key-recycling half in place.
questions.answer:
The dynamic endpoint removal (while the server is running) is not officially supported by FastAPI.
If you have a real-life use case where it would be useful, please open a new discussion and explain your use case. We will treat it as feature request

questions.title: Direct mutation of APIRouter.routes bypasses the routes-version cache, causing stale/ghost routes
questions.question:
Found via a property-based audit (copy/clone independence, cache-invalidation consistency) run across several widely-used Python libraries; repro was written and independently re-run twice (identical output both times) before filing.

## Description

Since the lazy/cached router-inclusion rewrite (#15745), `_IncludedRouter.effective_candidates()` (`fastapi/routing.py`) rebuilds and caches a resolved route list, gated by a version counter (`APIRouter._routes_version`, bumped by `_mark_routes_changed()`). Every *tracked* mutator (`add_route`, `add_api_route`, `add_websocket_route`, `add_api_websocket_route`, `include_router`) correctly bumps the counter, including recursively through nested includes.

However, `APIRouter.routes` is still a plain public `list` (inherited from `starlette.routing.Router`), and direct mutation of it is a documented pattern elsewhere (e.g. `app.router.routes = [...]` to remove routes). Directly mutating that list -- `router.routes.append(...)`, `.remove(...)`, `.clear()` -- does not call `_mark_routes_changed()`, so a parent router that already dispatched at least one request against an included child keeps serving from the stale cached candidate list, silently diverging from the router's actual current `.routes` contents.

This is a different root cause from #15974 (a concurrent-rebuild race, already fixed with `_effective_routes_lock`) -- that lock does nothing here, since the problem isn't concurrent rebuilding, it's that the version counter is never incremented at all for direct list mutation.

## Minimal repro

```python
from fastapi import APIRouter, FastAPI
from fastapi.routing import APIRoute
from starlette.testclient import TestClient

app = FastAPI()
child = APIRouter()

@child.get("/child")
def read_child():
    return {"msg": "v1-original"}

app.include_router(child, prefix="/api")
client = TestClient(app)

# Trigger dispatch once so the parent's _IncludedRouter builds and caches
# effective_candidates() at the current routes_version.
client.get("/api/child")

# Direction A: add a route directly to child.routes (bypass add_api_route).
def read_child2():
    return {"msg": "v2-added-directly"}

new_route = APIRoute("/child2", read_child2, methods=["GET"])
child.routes.append(new_route)  # no _mark_routes_changed() call happens here

r1 = client.get("/api/child2")
print(r1.status_code)  # actual: 404 -- expected: 200, it's literally in child.routes

# Direction B: remove the original route directly from child.routes.
original = [rt for rt in child.routes if getattr(rt, "path", None) == "/child"][0]
child.routes.remove(original)

r2 = client.get("/api/child")
print(r2.status_code)  # actual: 200 (ghost route) -- expected: 404, it was just removed
```

Output (run twice, identical both times):
```
after direct-append GET /api/child2 -> 404
after direct-remove GET /api/child -> 200
```

## Expected behavior

The parent router's effective route resolution should reflect the current contents of `child.routes` at request time.

## Actual behavior

Direct mutation of `.routes` after a router has been included and has served at least one request is silently ignored by the lazy cache -- an added route is invisible (404), and a removed route keeps being served as a "ghost" route (200).

## Versions

fastapi 0.140.0 (also confirmed present in `fastapi/routing.py` on `master` as of 2026-09-04), Python 3.12.10, Windows 11.
questions.answer:
Hello!

The direct mutation of `APIRouter.routes` at run time is not documented and therefore not officially supported by FastAPI.
If you need such feature, please open a [discussion](https://github.com/fastapi/fastapi/discussions/new?category=questions), describe the use case and we will treat it as feature request.

questions.question:
### First Check

### Commit to Help

- [X] I commit to help with one of those options 👆

### Example Code

```python
import time
from fastapi import BackgroundTasks, FastAPI

app = FastAPI()


def heavy_video_processing(video_id: str):
    # Simulating a heavy CPU task (takes 2 minutes)
    time.sleep(120)
    print(f"Finished processing video: {video_id}")


@app.post("/process-video/{video_id}")
async def process_video(video_id: str, background_tasks: BackgroundTasks):
    # Is using BackgroundTasks here recommended for production?
    background_tasks.add_task(heavy_video_processing, video_id)
    return {"status": "Processing started", "video_id": video_id}
```


### Description

What is the best practice architectural boundary for choosing between FastAPI's built-in BackgroundTasks versus an external task queue like Celery + Redis or ARQ?

I am building an API that needs to trigger long-running asynchronous jobs (like video processing or batch PDF generation). While BackgroundTasks works well in basic examples, I am concerned about process crashes, memory usage, worker blocking, and task durability when scaling in production.

### Operating System

Linux

### Operating System Details

Ubuntu 22.04 LTS (Running in Docker container on AWS ECS)

### FastAPI Version

0.110.0

### Pydantic Version

2.6.4

### Python Version

3.11.8

### Additional Context

_No response_
questions.answer:
For a 2-minute video processing job, I wouldn’t use `BackgroundTasks` in production.

`BackgroundTasks` runs inside the FastAPI process. That’s fine for small, non-critical work, but if the process restarts, crashes, or gets killed, the task is gone. It also isn’t a good place for CPU-heavy work.

For something like video processing or batch PDF generation, I’d put the job in a real worker queue:

* **ARQ + Redis** if you want something lightweight and async-friendly.
* **Celery + Redis/RabbitMQ** if you need a more mature ecosystem with things like retries, scheduling, and more complex workflows.

So I’d think about it less in terms of “how many seconds is too long?” and more in terms of **durability and resource usage**.

If losing the job is acceptable → `BackgroundTasks`.

If the job needs retries, survives deployments/restarts, or is resource-intensive → use a task queue.

questions.title: iter_route_contexts() yields an empty path for APIWebSocketRoute, so prefixed websocket routes cannot be enumerated
questions.question:
### Discussed in https://github.com/fastapi/fastapi/discussions/15782

### First Check

- [X] I added a very descriptive title here.
- [X] I used the GitHub search to find a similar issue and didn't find it.
- [X] I already searched in Google "How to X in FastAPI" and didn't find any information.
- [X] I already read and followed all the tutorial in the docs and didn't find an answer.
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Pydantic](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic).
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Swagger UI](https://github.com/swagger-api/swagger-ui).
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [ReDoc](https://github.com/Redocly/redoc).

### Description

`iter_route_contexts()` — the helper added in 0.137.2 (#15785) as the supported replacement for walking `router.routes` — yields `path == ""` for `APIWebSocketRoute`, while HTTP routes in the same router get their include prefix applied correctly.

The mounted path is not recoverable from anything the returned context exposes: `ctx.path` and `ctx.path_format` are both `""`, and `ctx.route.path` carries only the route's own un-prefixed path. So for an app that mounts websockets under a prefix, `iter_route_contexts()` cannot enumerate them at all.

This matters because `iter_route_contexts()` is the migration path being recommended to everyone whose route-introspection broke in 0.137 (instrumentation, metrics middleware, route-manifest generators, "is this endpoint mounted?" tests). Code that migrates to it as directed silently loses its websocket routes — the same failure mode as the original regression, just narrowed.

### Example Code

```python
from fastapi import APIRouter, FastAPI, WebSocket
from fastapi.routing import iter_route_contexts

router = APIRouter()


@router.get("/items")
def items():
    return {}


@router.websocket("/stream/{job_id}")
async def stream(websocket: WebSocket, job_id: str):
    await websocket.accept()


app = FastAPI()
app.include_router(router, prefix="/api/v1")

for ctx in iter_route_contexts(app.routes):
    route = getattr(ctx, "route", None)
    print(f"{ctx.path!r:<28} {type(route).__name__:<22} {getattr(route, 'path', None)!r}")
```

### Operating System

Windows

### FastAPI Version

0.141.1

### Python Version

3.13.14

### Additional Context

Output of the snippet above:

```
'/openapi.json'              Route                  '/openapi.json'
'/docs'                      Route                  '/docs'
'/docs/oauth2-redirect'      Route                  '/docs/oauth2-redirect'
'/redoc'                     Route                  '/redoc'
'/api/v1/items'              APIRoute               '/items'
''                           APIWebSocketRoute      '/stream/{job_id}'
```

Expected for the last row: `'/api/v1/stream/{job_id}'`, matching how `/api/v1/items` is resolved one row above.

**Full context object for the websocket entry**, showing the path is genuinely absent rather than stored elsewhere:

```
ctx.path            = ''
ctx.path_format     = ''
ctx.name            = ''
ctx.methods         = set()
ctx.route           = APIWebSocketRoute(path='/stream/{job_id}', ...)
ctx.original_route  = APIWebSocketRoute(path='/stream/{job_id}', ...)
ctx.endpoint        = None
```

The prefix does exist at `_IncludedRouter.include_context.prefix`, but `_RouterIncludeContext` is private, so there is no supported way for a caller to reassemble the path themselves.

Possibly related but a different surface: #16176 / #16051 concern `request.scope["route"].path` at *request* time (and note websockets *retained* prefixes there, while HTTP routes lost them). This report is about *introspection* time via `iter_route_contexts()`, where the asymmetry runs the other way.

Happy to open a PR if the maintainers agree on the intended behaviour — my read is that the websocket branch of the context-building should apply the include prefix the same way the HTTP branch does.
questions.answer: Thanks for the report! This should be handled by https://github.com/fastapi/fastapi/pull/16484 , which will be included in FastAPI 0.143.1 in the next few hours. :rocket:

questions.title: app.frontend()'s fallback existence check (_fallback_file_exists) blocks the event loop with synchronous I/O
questions.question:
### First Check

- [X] I added a very descriptive title here.
- [X] I used the GitHub search to find a similar question and didn't find it.
- [X] I searched the FastAPI documentation, with the integrated search.
- [X] I already searched in Google "How to X in FastAPI" and didn't find any information.
- [X] I already read and followed all the tutorial in the docs and didn't find an answer.
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Pydantic](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic).
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Swagger UI](https://github.com/swagger-api/swagger-ui).
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [ReDoc](https://github.com/Redocly/redoc).

### Commit to Help

- [X] I commit to help with one of those options 👆

### Example Code

```python
import os
import time
from pathlib import Path

_original_stat = os.stat


def _slow_stat(*args, **kwargs):
    time.sleep(0.2)  # simulate a slow filesystem stat() call
    return _original_stat(*args, **kwargs)


os.stat = _slow_stat

from fastapi import FastAPI  # noqa: E402

DIST_DIR = Path(__file__).parent / "dist"
DIST_DIR.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
(DIST_DIR / "index.html").write_text("app shell")

app = FastAPI()


@app.get("/api/fast")
async def fast_endpoint():
    return {"ok": True}


app.frontend("/", directory=DIST_DIR, fallback="auto")
```


### Description

The `_FrontendStaticFiles` class in `fastapi/routing.py` has a method `_fallback_file_exists`, used when `fallback="auto"` (the default) to check whether `404.html`/`index.html` exists in the frontend directory. This method calls `self.lookup_path(fallback)` directly, without `await`, which blocks the `asyncio` event loop for the duration of the filesystem call.

The sibling method `_lookup_path` (used for normal static file serving in the same class) offloads the equivalent filesystem call to a worker thread via `await run_in_threadpool(self.lookup_path, path)`. `_fallback_file_exists` does not follow the same pattern.

**What I expected**: since `fallback="auto"` is the default, and `_lookup_path` already offloads filesystem access to a thread pool elsewhere in the same class, I expected `_fallback_file_exists` to do the same.

**What's currently happening**: `_fallback_file_exists` runs `self.lookup_path()` synchronously inside an `async def` method with no `await`. On filesystems with meaningfully slow stat() calls (network filesystems, container overlay filesystems, etc.), a single request to a missing path can block every other request being served on the same event loop — including completely unrelated API endpoints — for the duration of the filesystem call.

Run the example code with `uvicorn repro:app --workers 1`, then send a burst of concurrent requests to a missing path (e.g. `/dashboard`) while measuring the latency of `/api/fast`. In my testing, `/api/fast` latency degraded substantially (hundreds of ms to multiple seconds) compared to a baseline with no concurrent frontend traffic. Happy to share the full benchmark harness and methodology if useful.

Proposed fix:

    async def _fallback_file_exists(self, fallback: str) -> bool:
        _, stat_result = await run_in_threadpool(self.lookup_path, fallback)
        return stat_result is not None and stat.S_ISREG(stat_result.st_mode)

The two call sites inside `get_response` would need an added `await`. `run_in_threadpool` is already imported in this file. Note: `_check_fallback_file` (called once at construction time for the startup-time directory check) is not part of the per-request hot path, so it's out of scope for this fix.

If this direction looks acceptable to the maintainers, I'd be happy to open a Pull Request with this change.

Python 3.12.10

This was found by reading through fastapi/routing.py looking for bugs in the recently added app.frontend() feature, then verified by patching the file locally to offload the call via run_in_threadpool and re-measuring. Happy to share the full benchmark harness (a FastAPI app + an async load-test script) if useful for verification.

questions.title: Clarify Union documentation for response_model in python 3.10+
questions.question:
### First Check

- [X] I added a very descriptive title here.
- [X] I used the GitHub search to find a similar question and didn't find it.
- [X] I searched the FastAPI documentation, with the integrated search.
- [X] I already searched in Google "How to X in FastAPI" and didn't find any information.
- [X] I already read and followed all the tutorial in the docs and didn't find an answer.
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Pydantic](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic).
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Swagger UI](https://github.com/swagger-api/swagger-ui).
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [ReDoc](https://github.com/Redocly/redoc).

### Commit to Help

- [X] I commit to help with one of those options 👆

### Example Code

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel

app = FastAPI()


class BaseItem(BaseModel):
    description: str
    type: str


class CarItem(BaseItem):
    type: str = "car"


class PlaneItem(BaseItem):
    type: str = "plane"
    size: int


items = {
    "item1": {"description": "All my friends drive a low rider", "type": "car"},
    "item2": {
        "description": "Music is my aeroplane, it's my aeroplane",
        "type": "plane",
        "size": 5,
    },
}


@app.get("/items/{item_id}", response_model=PlaneItem | CarItem)
async def read_item(item_id: str):
    return items[item_id]
```


### Description

I noticed a possible contradiction in the FastAPI documentation regarding `Union` and the use of the `|` operator with `response_model`.

In the Python 3.10+ example in the **"Union or anyOf"** section, the documentation uses:

```python
@app.get(
    "/items/{item_id}",
    response_model=PlaneItem | CarItem,
)
async def read_item(item_id: str):
    return items[item_id]
```

However, immediately below, in the **"Union in Python 3.10"** section, the documentation says:

> Because we are passing it as a value to an argument instead of putting it in a type annotation, we have to use `Union` even in Python 3.10.

It then states that using:

```python
response_model=PlaneItem | CarItem
```

would result in an error because Python would try to perform an invalid operation between `PlaneItem` and `CarItem` instead of interpreting it as a type annotation.

This seems contradictory because the Python 3.10+ example immediately above uses exactly `PlaneItem | CarItem` as the value of `response_model`.

I tested the example with a current Python/FastAPI setup, and:

```python
response_model=PlaneItem | CarItem
```

works as expected.

My understanding is that in Python 3.10+, `PlaneItem | CarItem` produces a union type at runtime, so it can be passed as the value of `response_model`. The fact that `response_model` is a runtime argument rather than a type annotation does not, by itself, mean that the `|` syntax cannot be used.

Could someone clarify whether the explanation in the **"Union in Python 3.10"** section is outdated, or whether there is some version-specific behavior that I am missing?

If the explanation is outdated, I would be happy to submit a documentation PR to clarify the wording and make the two sections consistent.

### Relevant documentation

The current Python 3.10+ example uses:

```python
response_model=PlaneItem | CarItem
```

while the following section says that the same syntax would result in an error and that `Union[...]` must be used.

I'm opening this discussion first to confirm the intended behaviour and documentation before proposing a PR. I'm happy to contribute a fix if needed

---

### Operating System

macOS

### Operating System Details

macOS Tahoe 26.6

### FastAPI Version

0.140.0

### Pydantic Version

2.13.4

### Python Version

3.10.20

### Additional Context

_No response_
questions.answer:
Ran the exact tutorial003_py310.py on fastapi 0.140.0 / pydantic 2.13.4 / py3.12 and it just works: item1 returns the car, item2 the plane with size, both 200, and the OpenAPI response schema comes out as anyOf of the two models. So the note is outdated. On 3.10+ `PlaneItem | CarItem` evaluates to a `types.UnionType` at runtime (PEP 604), which is exactly why passing it as the `response_model` value works.

The "must use Union, `|` would error" line is really pre-3.10 behavior, where `SomeClass | OtherClass` raises `TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for |` (confirmed on 3.9.6). The example file itself got switched to the `|` form in the 3.10 typing-syntax upgrade, but the surrounding text stayed, so they disagree now. Updating the prose to match the example looks like the right PR.

questions.title: Support specifying default values inside Annotated for parameter functions like Query()
questions.question:
### First Check

- [X] I added a very descriptive title here.
- [X] I used the GitHub search to find a similar question and didn't find it.
- [X] I searched the FastAPI documentation, with the integrated search.
- [X] I already searched in Google "How to X in FastAPI" and didn't find any information.
- [X] I already read and followed all the tutorial in the docs and didn't find an answer.
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Pydantic](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic).
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Swagger UI](https://github.com/swagger-api/swagger-ui).
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [ReDoc](https://github.com/Redocly/redoc).

### Commit to Help

- [X] I commit to help with one of those options 👆

### Example Code

```python
from typing import Annotated

from fastapi import FastAPI, Query

app = FastAPI()


@app.get("/items")
def read_items(
    limit: Annotated[
        int,
        Query(
            ge=1,
            le=100,
            description="Maximum number of items",
        ),
    ] = 10,
):
    return {"limit": limit}
```


### Description

While working with FastAPI and Pydantic v2, I noticed a difference in how defaults are specified when using `Annotated`.

With Pydantic, defaults can be declared inside `Field()`, which keeps all field-related configuration together:

```python
from typing import Annotated

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field


class Item(BaseModel):
    name: Annotated[
        str,
        Field(
            default="John",
            min_length=1,
        ),
    ]
```

However, FastAPI parameter helper functions such as `Query()` currently require the default value to be specified outside `Annotated`:

```python
from typing import Annotated

from fastapi import Query


limit: Annotated[
    int,
    Query(
        ge=1,
        le=100,
        description="Maximum number of items",
    ),
] = 10
```

I was wondering whether FastAPI could support an additional syntax such as:

```python
limit: Annotated[
    int,
    Query(
        default=10,
        ge=1,
        le=100,
        description="Maximum number of items",
    ),
]
```

or any equivalent approach.

I'm **not suggesting replacing the current syntax**. My question is whether this could be supported as an **additional, backward-compatible** option.

### Why I think it could be useful

- Keeps the default value together with the rest of the parameter metadata.
- Feels more consistent with Pydantic v2's `Field(default=...)` style.
- Improves readability for parameters with multiple validation constraints.
- Provides a single location for parameter configuration.

### My question

Is there an intentional design reason why FastAPI keeps the default value in the function signature instead of allowing it inside parameter helper functions like `Query()`, `Header()`, `Cookie()`, `Body()`, etc.?

Or could supporting this be considered as a future enhancement while preserving the current syntax?

Thanks!

### Operating System

macOS

### Operating System Details

MacOS Tahoe 26.5.2

### FastAPI Version

0.140.0

### Pydantic Version

2.13.4

### Python Version

3.14.6

### Additional Context

If this idea is considered a good fit for FastAPI, I'd be happy to contribute the implementation.
questions.answer:
It's mostly the latter: Pydantic can interpret the `Annotated` metadata at runtime, but that doesn't mean static type checkers understand a default placed inside it.

Pydantic's own docs call this out explicitly: `default`, `default_factory`, and `alias` affect the synthesized `__init__()`, but those arguments are **not understood by static type checkers when they're provided through the `Annotated` pattern**. For those cases, Pydantic recommends the normal assignment form instead.

So this:

```python
class Item(BaseModel):
    name: Annotated[str, Field(default="John")]
````

can be understood by Pydantic at runtime as having a default, but the `Field(...)` metadata itself doesn't redefine the annotation for a normal type checker.

That's also why the FastAPI/function case is more constrained:

```python
def read_items(
    limit: Annotated[int, Query(default=10)],
):
    ...
```

Regardless of how FastAPI interprets that metadata at runtime, Python's actual function signature still has **no default value** there:

```python
read_items()  # missing required argument
```

Whereas:

```python
def read_items(
    limit: Annotated[int, Query(ge=1, le=100)] = 10,
):
    ...
```

has a real Python default. That is visible to `inspect.signature()`, direct callers, IDEs, and static type checkers without any FastAPI-specific interpretation.

So Pydantic isn't getting a special general capability from `Annotated` that FastAPI could reuse here. Pydantic can consume the metadata while constructing a model at runtime, while FastAPI still has to preserve the semantics of an ordinary Python function signature.

Pydantic documents the static-checking limitation here:
[https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/concepts/fields/#the-annotated-pattern](https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/concepts/fields/#the-annotated-pattern)

FastAPI documents the same reason for keeping the real default outside `Query()` here:
[https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/query-params-str-validations/#query-as-the-default-value-or-in-annotated](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/query-params-str-validations/#query-as-the-default-value-or-in-annotated)

questions.title: Return type vs ORJSONResponse: does generic return type as dict[str, Any] use the Pydantic serializer efficently?
questions.question:
### First Check

- [X] I added a very descriptive title here.
- [X] I used the GitHub search to find a similar question and didn't find it.
- [X] I searched the FastAPI documentation, with the integrated search.
- [X] I already searched in Google "How to X in FastAPI" and didn't find any information.
- [X] I already read and followed all the tutorial in the docs and didn't find an answer.
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Pydantic](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic).
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Swagger UI](https://github.com/swagger-api/swagger-ui).
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [ReDoc](https://github.com/Redocly/redoc).

### Commit to Help

- [X] I commit to help with one of those options 👆

### Example Code

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI

app = FastAPI()

@app.get("/example")
def example() -> dict[str, Any]:
return {"hello": "world"}
```


### Description

Hi FastAPI team,
 
I have a question regarding the current response serialization behavior, especially after the recent ORJSONResponse deprecation guidance.
 
While investigating the warning:
 
> FastAPI now serializes data directly to JSON bytes via Pydantic when a return type or response model is set
 
I inspected the implementation of `fastapi.routing.serialize_response()` in the version currently installed in my environment and found the following logic:
 
```python
async def serialize_response(...):
if field:
...
serializer = field.serialize_json if dump_json else field.serialize
return serializer(...)
else:
return jsonable_encoder(response_content)
```
 
To better understand when the Pydantic serialization path is selected, I temporarily patched `serialize_response()` and logged the value of `field` during request execution.
 
For an endpoint defined only with a generic return type:
 
```python
@app.get("/example")
def example() -> dict[str, Any]:
return {"hello": "world"}
```
 
the runtime output was:
 
```text
ModelField(
field_info=FieldInfo(annotation=dict[str, Any], required=True),
name='Response_example',
mode='serialization',
config=None
)
```
 
This seems to indicate that FastAPI creates a response `ModelField` even for generic return types such as `dict[str, Any]`, and therefore enters the `field.serialize()` path instead of the `jsonable_encoder()` path.
 
Based on this, I would like to confirm a few points:
 
1. Is this behavior intentional and considered part of the public/expected behavior of FastAPI?
 
2. Can users rely on a generic return type like:
 
```python
-> dict[str, Any]
-> list[dict[str, Any]]
-> list[Any]
```
 
to activate the Pydantic response serialization path, even when no explicit `response_model` is provided?
 
3. From a performance perspective, should users generally prefer:
 
```python
@app.get("/")
def endpoint() -> dict[str, Any]:
...
```
 
over:
 
```python
@app.get("/", response_class=ORJSONResponse)
def endpoint():
...
```
 
given the current deprecation warning around `ORJSONResponse`?
 
4. Are there any meaningful performance differences between:
```python
-> dict[str, Any]
```
 
and
 
```python
-> MyPydanticModel
```
 
with regard to the generated serializer and serialization speed?
 
5. Would it be worth clarifying this point in the documentation?
 
The current wording mentions "return type or response model", which many readers (including me initially) could interpret as primarily referring to Pydantic models. However, from the implementation and runtime behavior it appears that even generic typed returns such as `dict[str, Any]` participate in the Pydantic serialization path.
 
Thanks for the clarification, and for all the work on FastAPI.

### Operating System

Linux

### Operating System Details

_No response_

### FastAPI Version

0.140.7

### Pydantic Version

2.13.4

### Python Version

Python 3.13.0

### Additional Context

_No response_
questions.answer:
Your reading of the code is right. Numbers below are from your exact versions — FastAPI 0.140.7, Pydantic 2.13.4, Python 3.13.

**1 and 2 — intentional, and yes you can rely on generics**

Any return annotation FastAPI can build a `TypeAdapter` for produces a response field, generics included:

```
route annotation                  response_field  response_class  fast path
-> (none)                         none            default         False
-> dict[str, Any]                 yes             default         True
-> list[dict[str, Any]]           yes             default         True
-> list[Any]                      yes             default         True
-> Any                            yes             default         True
-> MyModel                        yes             default         True
-> dict[str, Any] + ORJSONResponse yes            ORJSON          False
-> (none) + ORJSONResponse        none            ORJSON          False
```

Even bare `-> Any` gets one. The only ways to end up on the `jsonable_encoder` branch are to omit the annotation or to return a `Response` object yourself.

**3 — prefer the return type, and don't set both**

This is the part worth knowing. From `fastapi/routing.py` in 0.140.7:

```python
# Use the fast path (dump_json) when no custom response
# class was set and a response field with a TypeAdapter
# exists. Serializes directly to JSON bytes via Pydantic's
# Rust core, skipping the intermediate Python dict +
# json.dumps() step.
use_dump_json = response_field is not None and isinstance(
    response_class, DefaultPlaceholder
)
```

Passing `response_class=ORJSONResponse` means `response_class` is no longer a `DefaultPlaceholder`, so `use_dump_json` is `False` — you keep the response field but drop to `field.serialize` → Python objects → `ORJSONResponse.render()`. Setting both is the *slowest* of the three arrangements, not the fastest. (Both `ORJSONResponse` and `UJSONResponse` carry `@deprecated` in `fastapi/responses.py`, so the warning you hit is real, not advisory folklore.)

**4 — a model is faster than `dict[str, Any]`, and both beat the encoder path badly**

Serialization only, 20,000 iterations, best of 3, 20-key flat dict with one nested value:

```
 4.9 us   -> MyModel                        serialize_json  (fast path)
 6.1 us   -> dict[str, Any]                 serialize_json  (fast path)
13.3 us   -> dict[str, Any]                 serialize + json.dumps
48.4 us   no annotation + ORJSONResponse    jsonable_encoder + orjson.dumps
53.8 us   no annotation                     jsonable_encoder + json.dumps
 0.8 us   orjson.dumps(payload)             raw, for reference
```

The model wins by roughly 25% because `Any` has no static schema — pydantic-core has to infer each value's type at runtime, while a declared model compiles a specialized serializer.

The bigger point is the ~8x gap to the encoder rows, and it explains the deprecation: the expensive part was never `json.dumps` vs `orjson.dumps`, it was `jsonable_encoder` walking the object graph in Python. That's also why `ORJSONResponse` only ever bought ~10% here — it optimized the cheap half of the work. Absolute numbers scale with payload size and shape; the ratios held across runs.

**5 — agreed, worth documenting**

"return type or response model" is accurate but reads as if it means Pydantic models specifically. Two additions would have saved you the source dive: that *any* return annotation qualifies, `dict[str, Any]` included, and that setting a custom `response_class` silently opts you out of the fast path. The second one is the surprising half — it's easy to assume the two optimizations stack. Happy to open a docs PR if a maintainer wants it.
</content>

questions.title: jsonable_encoder drops exclude_defaults for dict values (propagated for list items)
questions.question:
### Summary

`jsonable_encoder` propagates `exclude_defaults` when recursing into **list/tuple/set items**, but silently drops it when recursing into **dict values** (and keys). The two sibling flags `exclude_unset` and `exclude_none` *are* forwarded in that same dict branch, so `exclude_defaults` is the lone omission. As a result the same Pydantic model, with the same flag, encodes differently depending on whether it sits inside a list or a dict.

### Where

`fastapi/encoders.py`, dict branch value recursion:

```python
encoded_value = jsonable_encoder(
    value,
    by_alias=by_alias,
    exclude_unset=exclude_unset,
    exclude_none=exclude_none,          # exclude_defaults is missing here
    custom_encoder=custom_encoder,
    sqlalchemy_safe=sqlalchemy_safe,
)
```

The list branch a few lines below passes `exclude_defaults=exclude_defaults`.

### Reproduction (real `fastapi.encoders.jsonable_encoder`, pydantic 2.x)

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel
from fastapi.encoders import jsonable_encoder

class M(BaseModel):
    a: int = 5
    b: int = 10

jsonable_encoder([M()], exclude_defaults=True)        # [{}]                     -> defaults stripped
jsonable_encoder({"k": M()}, exclude_defaults=True)   # {"k": {"a": 5, "b": 10}} -> NOT stripped
```

Same model, same flag, different result purely by container type.

### Proposed fix

Add `exclude_defaults=exclude_defaults` to the dict-branch recursion (value, and for parity the key), matching the list branch and the two sibling flags already forwarded there:

```python
encoded_value = jsonable_encoder(
    value,
    by_alias=by_alias,
    exclude_unset=exclude_unset,
    exclude_defaults=exclude_defaults,
    exclude_none=exclude_none,
    custom_encoder=custom_encoder,
    sqlalchemy_safe=sqlalchemy_safe,
)
```

### Notes

`exclude_defaults` is a documented public parameter of `jsonable_encoder`. The default FastAPI response path calls it with `exclude_defaults=False`, so this doesn't affect default responses — it surfaces for direct `jsonable_encoder(..., exclude_defaults=True)` use (and internal callers passing the flag). Filing as a Discussion per the contributing guidelines — happy to open a PR with the one-line fix (and a test) if a maintainer would like.

questions.title: Invalid `contact`/`license_info` URL fails lazily at first /openapi.json request, not at app construction — confusing traceback
questions.question:
### First Check

- [X] I added a very descriptive title here.
- [X] I used the GitHub search to find a similar question and didn't find it.
- [X] I searched the FastAPI documentation, with the integrated search.
- [X] I already searched in Google "How to X in FastAPI" and didn't find any information.
- [X] I already read and followed all the tutorial in the docs and didn't find an answer.
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Pydantic](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic).
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Swagger UI](https://github.com/swagger-api/swagger-ui).
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [ReDoc](https://github.com/Redocly/redoc).

### Commit to Help

- [X] I commit to help with one of those options 👆

### Example Code

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI

app = FastAPI(
    contact={"name": "Test", "url": "/relative-path"}  # invalid - not absolute
)

@app.get("/health")
def health():
    return {"status": "ok"}

# App starts successfully with no warning.
# GET /health works fine.
# GET /openapi.json (or /docs) throws:
#   pydantic_core._pydantic_core.ValidationError: 1 validation error for OpenAPI
#   info.contact.url
#     Input should be a valid URL, relative URL without a base [type=url_parsing, ...]
# ...5 layers deep through Starlette's exception_handler/routing internals.
```


### Description

FastAPI accepts `contact={"url": ...}` (and `license_info`) at app 
construction time without validating the URL. The value is only actually 
validated by Pydantic the first time `/openapi.json` is requested — meaning 
a mistake made when constructing `FastAPI(...)` doesn't surface until a 
completely unrelated request happens later, and then as a 500 error buried 
five layers deep in Starlette's exception handling, rather than a clear 
error pointing at the actual mistake.

### Operating System

macOS

### Operating System Details

macOS (Apple Silicon), Python 3.12, running in AWS Lambda (Amazon Linux 2023 runtime) via Mangum in production; reproduced locally on macOS as well.

### FastAPI Version

0.115.0

### Pydantic Version

v2

### Python Version

3.12

### Additional Context

This surfaced in a real deployment scenario — I build contact.url dynamically based on environment (e.g. a stable production domain vs. a per-deployment execute-api URL), and one code path produced a relative string by accident. The mistake was made at FastAPI() construction time, but nothing surfaced until a completely unrelated later request to /docs — which made the actual cause much harder to trace back to its source than it should have been.

Since contact/license_info aren't validated until the first /openapi.json request, the app starts successfully and every other endpoint works fine — the failure only appears later, on a request that has nothing to do with where the actual mistake was made. The traceback also goes five layers deep through Starlette's exception-handling internals before reaching the real Pydantic error, which makes it easy to misdiagnose as a framework or Starlette bug rather than a simple app-construction typo.
questions.answer:
The contact.url only gets validated when the OpenAPI model is built, at `OpenAPI(**output)` at the end of openapi/utils.py. FastAPI() stores it as a raw dict at construction and builds the schema lazily on the first /openapi.json or /docs hit, then caches it, so nothing else trips over it first.

Want it to fail at startup? call app.openapi() once right after you construct the app. Same ValidationError on info.contact.url, just where the typo actually is. Checked on 0.115.0, unchanged on master.

questions.title: app.frontend() with fallback="index.html" returns 404 for client side routes that have a dot in the last path segment (like /users/john.doe or /v/1.2.3)
questions.question:
### First Check

- [x] I added a very descriptive title here.
- [x] I used the GitHub search to find a similar question and didn't find it.
- [x] I searched the FastAPI documentation, with the integrated search.
- [x] I already searched in Google "How to X in FastAPI" and didn't find any information.
- [x] I already read and followed all the tutorial in the docs and didn't find an answer.
- [x] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to Pydantic.
- [x] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to Swagger UI.
- [x] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to ReDoc.

### Commit to Help

- [x] I commit to help with one of those options 👆

### Example Code

```python
import os
import tempfile

from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient

dist = tempfile.mkdtemp()
with open(os.path.join(dist, "index.html"), "w") as f:
    f.write("<html>SPA shell</html>")

app = FastAPI()
app.frontend("/", directory=dist, fallback="index.html")

client = TestClient(app)

# The Accept header a browser sends on a normal top level navigation.
browser_nav = {
    "accept": "text/html,application/xhtml+xml,application/xml;q=0.9,"
    "image/avif,image/webp,image/apng,*/*;q=0.8"
}

print(client.get("/users/john", headers=browser_nav).status_code)      # 200, serves index.html
print(client.get("/users/john.doe", headers=browser_nav).status_code)  # 404
print(client.get("/v/1.2.3", headers=browser_nav).status_code)         # 404
```

### Description

Hi 👋

I have been trying out the new `app.frontend()` helper to serve a single page app, using `fallback="index.html"` so that client side routes fall back to the shell and the frontend router can take over. This is the behavior described in the "Client side routing" part of the docs, and it works fine for a path like `/dashboard` or `/dashboard/settings`.

The problem shows up when a client side route has a dot in its last path segment. Plenty of real apps have these, for example a profile at `/users/john.doe`, a version deep link at `/v/1.2.3`, or a slug like `/files/report.2024`. When I open one of those directly, or just hit refresh while I am already on that page, I get a 404 instead of the `index.html` shell, so the app never loads and the client router never gets a chance to handle the route.

The part that surprised me is that setting `fallback="index.html"` explicitly does not change this. As far as I can tell there is currently no way to get these routes to fall back to the shell.

I spent some time reading the code and I think it comes from `_is_frontend_navigation_request()` in `fastapi/routing.py`. It takes the last path segment and if `os.path.splitext(...)` finds an extension it returns early and treats the request as an asset request, before it ever looks at the `Accept` header. Because `os.path.splitext("john.doe")` returns `.doe`, any segment with a dot in it is treated as a file and never gets the `index.html` fallback, even when the browser clearly asked for `text/html`.

What makes me think this is fixable without regressions is that the two situations are easy to tell apart. A real browser navigation sends `Accept: text/html`, while a missing asset requested from a script tag, an image tag, or a fetch call sends `*/*` or a specific type like `text/css`. If I request a genuinely missing asset such as `/assets/missing.js` with `Accept: */*` it still returns 404 as expected, so checking the `Accept` header first would fix the navigation case and keep the asset case working.

I did notice there is already a test that pins the current behavior. `test_index_fallback_does_not_handle_asset_like_or_non_html_requests` has a `("/users/jane.doe", "text/html")` case that expects a 404, so before proposing a change I wanted to ask whether the current behavior is intentional. If the idea is that dotted client routes should be servable, would a change that treats an explicit `Accept: text/html` request as navigation regardless of the path be acceptable? Or would you rather keep the extension heuristic as the default for `fallback="auto"` and add an opt in for apps that use dotted client side routes?

I am happy to open a PR with a failing test and the change for whichever direction you prefer. Thanks a lot for the work on this feature.

### Operating System

Windows

### Operating System Details

Also reproduced on current master. The logic involved is pure routing code, so it is not tied to any particular operating system.

### FastAPI Version

0.139.0

### Pydantic Version

2.13.4

### Python Version

3.11

### Additional Context

_No response_
questions.answer:
Thank you for the clear report!

Indeed, this should be fixed. I'm tracking it here in this issue for completeness: https://github.com/fastapi/fastapi/issues/16010 , and fix PR here: https://github.com/fastapi/fastapi/pull/16011

### Commit to Help

- [X] I commit to help with one of those options 👆

### Example Code

```python
import asyncio
from fastapi.concurrency import contextmanager_in_threadpool


class TrackingCM:
    """Context manager that tracks whether __exit__ is called."""
    
    def __init__(self, name: str):
        self.name = name
        self.exit_called = False
    
    def __enter__(self):
        print(f"  [{self.name}] __enter__ called")
        raise ValueError("setup failed")
    
    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc_val, exc_tb):
        self.exit_called = True
        print(f"  [{self.name}] __exit__ called  <-- PEP 343 violation!")


async def main():
    print("=" * 70)
    print("Behavioral inconsistency with Python context manager protocol")
    print("=" * 70)
    
    print("\n1. Standard Python `with`:")
    cm1 = TrackingCM("standard")
    try:
        with cm1:
            pass
    except ValueError:
        pass
    print(f"   Result: exit_called = {cm1.exit_called}")
    print(f"   OK: __exit__ NOT called when __enter__ raises")
    
    print("\n2. contextmanager_in_threadpool:")
    cm2 = TrackingCM("threadpool")
    try:
        async with contextmanager_in_threadpool(cm2):
            pass
    except ValueError:
        pass
    print(f"   Result: exit_called = {cm2.exit_called}")
    if cm2.exit_called:
        print(f"   FAIL: __exit__ IS called when __enter__ raises")
    
    print("\n" + "=" * 70)
    print("Root cause:")
    print("=" * 70)
    print("In fastapi/concurrency.py:")
    print("  try:")
    print("      yield await run_in_threadpool(cm.__enter__)  # if raises -> except")
    print("  except Exception as e:")
    print("      ok = bool(await anyio.to_thread.run_sync(cm.__exit__, ...))")
    print("")
    print("When __enter__ raises, the exception falls into `except`, and __exit__")
    print("is called. In standard Python `with`, if __enter__ raises, __exit__ is")
    print("NOT called (the context was never entered).")
    print("=" * 70)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())
```


### Description

I`m wrapping a sync context manager with contextmanager_in_threadpool. When __enter__ raises, I expect __exit__ to NOT be called, per PEP 343 (the context was never entered). Instead, __exit__ IS called. See the Minimal Reproducible Example (MRE).

### Operating System

Linux

Ubuntu 24.04 LTS
