- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Swagger UI](https://github.com/swagger-api/swagger-ui).
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [ReDoc](https://github.com/Redocly/redoc).

### Commit to Help

- [X] I commit to help with one of those options 👆

### Example Code

```python
from functools import wraps
import uvicorn
from fastapi import FastAPI

app = FastAPI()

def my_decorator(func):
    """A decorator that wraps a sync function with an async handler."""

    @wraps(func)
    async def wrapper():
        func()
        return 'OK'

    return wrapper

@app.get('/')
@my_decorator
def index():
    """A simple sync page function."""
    print('Hello!')

if __name__ == '__main__':
    uvicorn.run(app)
```


### Description

* Visit "/".
* You'll see "Internal Server Error".
* A ValueError appears:
    ```
    ValueError: [TypeError("'coroutine' object is not iterable"), TypeError('vars() argument must have __dict__ attribute')]
    ```

Since FastAPI 0.123.5 (PR #14434), using `functools.wraps` on an async wrapper around a sync function causes FastAPI to incorrectly treat the handler as sync, resulting in: `ValueError: [TypeError("'coroutine' object is not iterable"), ...]`

The issue is that `Dependant.is_coroutine_callable` now uses `inspect.unwrap()` which follows `__wrapped__` back to the original sync function, instead of checking if the actual registered handler is async.

### Operating System

macOS

### Operating System Details

_No response_

### FastAPI Version

0.123.5

### Pydantic Version

2.12.5

### Python Version

3.11.11

_No response_

questions.answer: `example` property is deprecated by openapi specification. FastAPI just follows the specification. See: https://spec.openapis.org/oas/v3.1.0#fixed-fields-19 --- Use `examples` and `openapi_examples`: ```py from typing import Annotated from fastapi import FastAPI, Path from pydantic import BaseModel, Field class MY_OBJ(BaseModel): id: Annotated[int, Field(examples=[5])] name: Annotated[int, Field(examples=["object name example"])] app = FastAPI() @app.get("/v0/my_obj/{objectid}") def get_my_obj( objectid: int = Path(..., openapi_examples={"example1": {"value": 5}}), ) -> list[MY_OBJ]: pass ```

questions.answer:
Requirements line: "starlette>=0.40.0,<0.51.0"

CVE affected versions: "starlette>= 0.39.0, <= 0.49.0"

As most of package managers prefer latest possible version during dependency resolution,  this will lead to installing 0.49.1 or 0.50.0 which are not affected by this CVE.

Cases then version with CVE is installed:
* Starlette version is limited by some other dependency
* Starlette version is explicitly limited by user
* Starlette was installed long time ago into venv, and no package updates were performed since

Releasing FastAPI with lower version limit bumped will not change anything in these 3 cases. If user wants to use specific Starlette version, of cannot upgrade, nothin will change.
It's not a FastAPI job to perform vulnerability scans or maintenance for dependencies used in user project.

Input validations work normally at the same time. I'm not sure if this is a bug. ### Operating System Linux ### Operating System Details _No response_ ### FastAPI Version 0.121.3 ### Pydantic Version 2.12.4 ### Python Version 3.12.7 ### Additional Context _No response_
questions.answer:
By default, Pydantic would expect to validate the external data received when creating a model, but it will assume that if you set values in your own code, that code is already correct and has correct values.

If you're in a situation where you cannot trust the assignment of the values in the model from inside your same code, you can change the Pydantic model to also validate on assignment: https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/api/config/#pydantic.config.ConfigDict.validate_assignment

This way it will raise a validation error that will become a server error right on the first line where the first incorrect value is set.

For example:

```Python
from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel, EmailStr, Field

app = FastAPI()


class UserIn(BaseModel):
    email: EmailStr
    age: int = Field(default=18, gt=0)
    not_null: str

    model_config = {"validate_assignment": True}


@app.post("/user/", response_model=UserIn)
async def create_user(user: UserIn) -> UserIn:
    user.email = "invalid email"
    user.age = -1
    user.not_null = None
    return user
```

Notice the:

```Python
    model_config = {"validate_assignment": True}
```

questions.title: Dependency injection fails for callable instances with PEP 563 annotations
questions.question: ### First Check - [X] I added a very descriptive title here. - [X] I used the GitHub search to find a similar question and didn't find it. - [X] I searched the FastAPI documentation, with the integrated search. - [x] I already searched in Google "How to X in FastAPI" and didn't find any information. - [X] I already read and followed all the tutorial in the docs and didn't find an answer. - [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Pydantic](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic). - [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Swagger UI](https://github.com/swagger-api/swagger-ui). - [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [ReDoc](https://github.com/Redocly/redoc). ### Commit to Help - [X] I commit to help with one of those options 👆 ### Example Code ```python from __future__ import annotations from typing import Annotated from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI, Request app = FastAPI() def get_dependency() -> str: return "injected_value" # FAILS: Callable instance class CallableAuth: def __init__(self, privileges: list[str]): self.privileges = privileges async def __call__(self, request: Request, dep: Annotated[str, Depends(get_dependency)]): # ...do auth work return {"dep": dep} # WORKS: Plain function async def function_auth(request: Request, dep: Annotated[str, Depends(get_dependency)]): return {"dep": dep} @app.get("/class") async def with_class(auth: Annotated[dict, Depends(CallableAuth(["SUPER_ADMIN", "ADMIN"]))]): return auth # Fails: Field required for 'dep' (treated as query param) @app.get("/function") async def with_function(auth: Annotated[dict, Depends(function_auth)]): return auth # Works correctly ``` ### Description * Open the browser and go to `/docs`. You'll find an error fetching the /openapi.json Error: ``` pydantic.errors.PydanticUserError: 'TypeAdapter[typing.Annotated[ForwardRef('Request'), Query(PydanticUndefined)]]' is not fully defined; you should define 'typing.Annotated[ForwardRef('Request'), Query(PydanticUndefined)]' and all referenced types, then call '.rebuild()' on the instance. For further information visit https://errors.pydantic.dev/2.11/u/class-not-fully-defined ``` Submit a cURL to test the endpoint, ``` curl --location '{your-dev-server}/class' ``` Response: ```json { "detail": [ { "type": "missing", "loc": [ "query", "request" ], "msg": "Field required", "input": null }, { "type": "missing", "loc": [ "query", "dep" ], "msg": "Field required", "input": null } ] } ``` ### Operating System Windows ### Operating System Details _No response_ ### FastAPI Version 0.118.0 ### Pydantic Version 2.11.10 ### Python Version Python 3.13.3 ### Additional Context ## Context I discovered a bug in FastAPI's dependency injection system that affects callable instances when using `from __future__ import annotations` (PEP 563). Since this will become the default behavior in Python 3.14, I wanted to bring it to your attention. ## The Issue When passing a callable instance (an object with `__call__`) to `Depends()`, FastAPI incorrectly treats dependency parameters as query parameters instead of sub-dependencies. This only happens when `from __future__ import annotations` is present. ## Root Cause In `fastapi/dependencies/utils.py`, the `get_typed_signature()` function extracts `__globals__` to resolve string annotations: ```python def get_typed_signature(call: Callable[..., Any]) -> inspect.Signature: signature = inspect.signature(call) globalns = getattr(call, "__globals__", {}) # Returns {} for instances! ``` The problem: - For functions: `getattr(func, "__globals__", {})` returns the module's globals ✅ - For instances: `getattr(instance, "__globals__", {})` returns `{}` because instances don't have `__globals__` ❌ - With empty globals, Pydantic's `try_eval_type()` can't resolve `ForwardRef('Annotated[str, Depends(...)]')` - FastAPI receives unresolved `ForwardRef` objects, can't find the `Depends()` marker, and falls back to treating them as query parameters ## Proposed Fix ```python def get_typed_signature(call: Callable[..., Any]) -> inspect.Signature: signature = inspect.signature(call) globalns = getattr(call, "__globals__", {}) # For callable instances, get __globals__ from the __call__ method if not globalns and hasattr(call, "__call__"): globalns = getattr(call.__call__, "__globals__", {}) typed_params = [ inspect.Parameter( name=param.name, kind=param.kind, default=param.default, annotation=get_typed_annotation(param.annotation, globalns), ) for param in signature.parameters.values() ] typed_signature = inspect.Signature(typed_params) return typed_signature ``` This fix: - Only activates when `__globals__` is empty (no impact on working cases) - Correctly extracts globals from the `__call__` method - Is minimal and safe ## Why This Matters 1. **Python 3.14**: PEP 563 becomes default, making this bug affect everyone 2. **Documented feature**: FastAPI docs show callable classes work with `Depends()` 3. **Common pattern**: Many users use callable classes for stateful dependencies, as seen in the example above used in the Example Code. ## Testing I've verified the fix resolves the issue. I'm happy to submit a PR with test cases if you'd like.
questions.answer: This was fixed by https://github.com/fastapi/fastapi/pull/11355, works well with FastAPI 0.123.7+

### Example Code

```python
# routers/one.py
from fastapi import APIRouter
from pydantic import BaseModel

router = APIRouter(prefix="/one")


class Data(BaseModel):
    state: str


class Response(BaseModel):
    data: Data


@router.get(
    "",
    response_model=Response,
)
def get__one():
    pass

#routers/two.py
from fastapi import APIRouter
from pydantic import BaseModel

router = APIRouter(prefix="/two")


class Data(BaseModel):
    state: str


class Response(BaseModel):
    data: Data


@router.get(
    "",
    response_model=Response,
)
def get__two():
    pass

#app.py
from fastapi import FastAPI

from routers import one, two


app = FastAPI()

app.include_router(one.router)
app.include_router(two.router)

#script.py
from pathlib import Path

import json

from app import app


def generate(check: bool = False):
    path = Path("openapi.json")

    openapi_schema = app.openapi()
    with path.open("w") as f:
        json.dumps(f, indent=2)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    generate()
```


### Description

https://github.com/fastapi/fastapi/blob/456008a52b01b570a0f03f8c9d53722eda137728/fastapi/_compat/v2.py#L304-L313

We are generating the openapi spec similar to the MRE above. When the JSON Schema is generated any models with a shared schema will have a shared ref. In the example above the definitions refs before remapping look like

```
{'$ref': '#/components/schemas/routers__one__Response'}, 
{'$ref': '#/components/schemas/routers__two__Response'}, 
{'$ref': '#/components/schemas/Data'}, 
```

As these are remapped, the old name `"Data"` is mapped to either `"router__one__Data"` or `"router__two__Data"` in a non-deterministic way. We check in CI for any changes to the spec and this is causing our CI to be unreliable.

The field-mapping here could be sorted which would at least make it deterministic, but I appreciate this is a little fiddly so I thought I would just open a discussion here?

In the mean-time we are adding docstrings to affected models to disambiguate their json-schema.

questions.answer:
hey @mattalexanderhill, 

OpenAPI spec generation should be deterministic. You are correct on that. Even though modern Python preserves insertion order, reliance on dictionary iteration order during complex recursive schema mapping is fragile and frequently breaks CI pipelines like yours.

Since you have already identified the loop causing the non-determinism (`field_mapping.items()`), I strongly encourage you to **submit a PR to sort it**.
Simply changing the iteration to `sorted(field_mapping.items(), key=lambda x: x[0].__name__)` (or a similar stable key) would likely solve this for the whole community. It is a valid bug that the spec generation fluctuates.

The issue is triggered because FastAPI detects a naming collision (`Response` vs `Response`) and enters that fallback resolution logic to generate the `routers__one__Response` names.

To unblock your CI immediately, the most robust fix is to bypass that collision logic entirely by ensuring the classes have unique names at the Python class definition level:

```python
# routers/one.py
class OneResponse(BaseModel): # Renamed from Response
    data: Data

# routers/two.py
class TwoResponse(BaseModel): # Renamed from Response
    data: Data
```

I know this is similar to "Option 2" mentioned above, but it really is the only way to guarantee stability until the framework patch lands. Using `model_config` often isn't enough because FastAPI uses the class `__name__` to generate the `$ref` keys in `components/schemas`, which is where the collision resolution logic kicks in.

**If you find this breakdown helpful for your debugging, please mark this response as the answer so others with similar OpenAPI spec generation needs can find it easily\!**

questions.title: Possible memory leak when using UploadFile
questions.question: ### First Check - [X] I added a very descriptive title here. - [X] I used the GitHub search to find a similar question and didn't find it. - [X] I searched the FastAPI documentation, with the integrated search. - [X] I already searched in Google "How to X in FastAPI" and didn't find any information. - [X] I already read and followed all the tutorial in the docs and didn't find an answer. - [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Pydantic](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic). - [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Swagger UI](https://github.com/swagger-api/swagger-ui). - [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [ReDoc](https://github.com/Redocly/redoc). ### Commit to Help - [x] I commit to help with one of those options 👆 ### Example Code ```python @router.post("/projects", response_model=ProjectResponse, operation_id="projects_create") async def api_projects_create( request: fastapi.Request, name: Annotated[str, fastapi.Form()], software_name: Annotated[str, fastapi.Form()], skip_project_setup: Annotated[bool, fastapi.Form()] = False, project_setup_payload: Annotated[Json, fastapi.Form()] = {}, setup_files: Annotated[list[fastapi.UploadFile], fastapi.File()] = [], ): for input_file in setup_files: output_path = Path('sample_folder') / some_random_name() async with aiofiles.open(output_path, "wb") as out_file: while True: chunk = await input_file.read(CHUNK_FILE_SIZE) if not chunk: break await out_file.write(chunk) ``` ### Description I'm using UploadFile, for handling the upload of some files, in an endpoint like the one reported above. The endpoint is not exacly like that but the reported snippet it's pretty similar regarding what we do with the files. It's probably a specific use case because we have both Form and a list of UploadFile (that I'm not sure I've annotated correctly). The issue is that, even if I'm using UploadFile, the uploaded files seems to be loaded partially in RAM and never ever properly freed, even after minutes. > at 9:57 you can see the upload > here's the same with two uploads: one at 10:18, the second at 10:21. The memory delta is almost exacly the half of the size of the uploaded file We've done some investigations to search for a possible memory leak. First we created a FileUploadContext to ensure all files are closed in the endpoint: ```python class UploadFilesContext: def __init__(self, files: list[UploadFile]) -> None: self.files = files async def __aenter__(self): return self.files async def __aexit__(self, exc_type, exc_value, exc_tb): for file in self.files: try: await file.close() except BaseException: logging.exception("Unable to properly close file from UploadFilesContext") @router.post("/projects", response_model=ProjectResponse, operation_id="projects_create") async def api_projects_create( request: fastapi.Request, name: Annotated[str, fastapi.Form()], software_name: Annotated[str, fastapi.Form()], skip_project_setup: Annotated[bool, fastapi.Form()] = False, project_setup_payload: Annotated[Json, fastapi.Form()] = {}, setup_files: Annotated[list[fastapi.UploadFile], fastapi.File()] = [], ): async with UploadFilesContext(setup_files) as setup_files: ... # the rest like before ``` At this point we are pretty sure that all UploadFiles should be closed using the `close()` method. We have tried to check up memory references to sus classes: ```python async def test_debug(): data = {} for cls in ["UploadFile", "SpooledTemporaryFile", "BytesIO", "IO"]: data[cls] = objgraph.count(cls) objgraph.show_backrefs( objgraph.by_type("SpooledTemporaryFile")[:1], max_depth=5, filename=f"{uuid4()}.png" ) return data ``` And sometime we noticed that a SpooledTemporaryFile reference was hanging. Going further this should be the references tree: That might be related to this part of starlette code: https://github.com/Kludex/starlette/blob/main/starlette/datastructures.py#L478 and https://github.com/Kludex/starlette/blob/main/starlette/concurrency.py#L30 - Is it possible that FormData or UploadFile is memory leaking somewhere? - Is it correct to use list[UploadFile] like I did in the snippet? - Should I care to handle closing other resources from the endpoint? ### Operating System Linux ### Operating System Details Mainly happens inside a Docker context. ### FastAPI Version 0.121.2 ### Pydantic Version 2.12.4 ### Python Version 3.11.13 ### Additional Context _No response_
questions.answer:
Hi @gbertoncelli-nw,

The `objgraph` trace pointing to `run_in_threadpool` is the key indicator here.

**The likely cause**
When you loop through the file with `await input_file.read(CHUNK_FILE_SIZE)`, you are dispatching a new task to the threadpool for *every single chunk*. For a large file, this creates thousands of short-lived thread tasks. This puts immense pressure on the `anyio` and `starlette` threadpool and the Python Garbage Collector, often leading to memory fragmentation or "soft leaks" where objects (like the captured `self.file` reference in the thread task) stay alive longer than expected.

**Solution**
Since `UploadFile` wraps a synchronous `SpooledTemporaryFile`, it is most efficient to perform the file copy completely synchronously within a *single* threadpool task, rather than switching back and forth between async and sync contexts for every chunk.

Try replacing your read/write loop with `shutil.copyfileobj` wrapped in `run_in_threadpool`. This moves the heavy lifting to a worker thread and keeps the main loop clean.

```python
import shutil
from starlette.concurrency import run_in_threadpool

# Define a sync helper function to do the copy
def save_file_sync(input_file_obj, output_path):
    with open(output_path, "wb") as buffer:
        shutil.copyfileobj(input_file_obj, buffer)

# Inside your endpoint
for input_file in setup_files:
    output_path = Path('sample_folder') / some_random_name()
    
    # Ensure the file cursor is at the start (just in case)
    await input_file.seek(0)
    
    # Run the blocking copy operation in a separate thread
    await run_in_threadpool(save_file_sync, input_file.file, output_path)
```

**your questions**

**Is `FormData` or `UploadFile` memory leaking?**
    Likely not the classes themselves, but the *usage pattern* involving thousands of `run_in_threadpool` calls creates references that are hard for the GC to clean up immediately. The `objgraph` references you see are likely the closures created for these thread tasks.

**Is it correct to use `list[UploadFile]`?**
    Yes, your annotation `Annotated[list[fastapi.UploadFile], fastapi.File()]` is correct. `python-multipart` handles this standardly.

*Should I care to handle closing other resources?**
    Your `UploadFilesContext` is excellent practice. However, if you switch to the `shutil` method above, you might find the manual closing is still necessary but the memory pressure will disappear because you aren't generating the massive object overhead during the read.

questions.question:

- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [ReDoc](https://github.com/Redocly/redoc).

### Commit to Help

- [X] I commit to help with one of those options 👆

### Example Code

```python
"""
  The NoSQL tutorial (docs_src/nosql_databases/tutorial001_scylla.py) demonstrates
  FastAPI integration with ScyllaDB:
  """

  from contextlib import asynccontextmanager
  from typing import List, Union
  from uuid import UUID, uuid4
  from cassandra.cluster import Cluster
  from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI, HTTPException
  from pydantic import BaseModel, Field


  class TaskBase(BaseModel):
      title: str
      description: Union[str, None] = None
      status: str = "pending"


  class TaskCreate(TaskBase):
      pass


  class Task(TaskBase):
      id: UUID = Field(default_factory=uuid4)


  class ScyllaDBConnection:
      def __init__(self, hosts=["scylladb"], port=9042):
          self.cluster = Cluster(hosts, port=port)
          self.session = None
          self.keyspace = "task_manager"

      def connect(self):
          self.session = self.cluster.connect()
          self.create_keyspace()
          self.session.set_keyspace(self.keyspace)
          self.create_table()

      def create_keyspace(self):
          self.session.execute(
              f"""
              CREATE KEYSPACE IF NOT EXISTS {self.keyspace}
              WITH replication = {{'class': 'SimpleStrategy', 'replication_factor': 1}}
              """
          )

      def create_table(self):
          self.session.execute(
              """
              CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS tasks (
                  id uuid PRIMARY KEY,
                  title text,
                  description text,
                  status text,
                  created_at timestamp,
                  updated_at timestamp
              )
              """
          )

      def close(self):
          if self.session:
              self.session.shutdown()
          if self.cluster:
              self.cluster.shutdown()


  db = ScyllaDBConnection()


  @asynccontextmanager
  async def lifespan(app: FastAPI):
      db.connect()
      yield
      db.close()


  app = FastAPI(lifespan=lifespan)


  def get_db():
      return db.session


  @app.post("/tasks/", response_model=Task)
  def create_task(task: TaskCreate, session=Depends(get_db)):
      task_id = uuid4()
      query = """
          INSERT INTO tasks (id, title, description, status, created_at, updated_at)
          VALUES (%s, %s, %s, %s, toTimestamp(now()), toTimestamp(now()))
      """
      session.execute(query, (task_id, task.title, task.description, task.status))
      return Task(id=task_id, **task.model_dump())


  @app.get("/tasks/", response_model=List[Task])
  def read_tasks(session=Depends(get_db)):
      query = "SELECT id, title, description, status FROM tasks"
      rows = session.execute(query)
      return [
          Task(id=row.id, title=row.title, description=row.description, status=row.status)
          for row in rows
      ]
```


### Description

FastAPI documentation currently doesn't mention NoSQL database integration, even though FastAPI works well with NoSQL databases like ScyllaDB, Cassandra, MongoDB, Redis, etc.

**The problem:**
- FastAPI has excellent SQL database tutorials (SQLModel, SQLAlchemy)
- NoSQL databases are not mentioned anywhere in the official documentation
- Developers assume FastAPI only works with SQL databases or need to search elsewhere

**What's already happening in the community:**
- Community articles demonstrate FastAPI + Cassandra integration:
https://dev.to/csar_fabinchvezlinar/building-a-task-management-api-with-apache-cassandra-and-fastapi-3ho0
- DataStax Astra DB has FastAPI integration docs:
https://awesome-astra.github.io/docs/pages/develop/frameworks/fastapi/
- Developers are successfully using FastAPI with NoSQL in production

**What could happen instead:**
- FastAPI docs should include a NoSQL databases tutorial (similar to the SQL tutorial)
- Demonstrate integration with ScyllaDB/Cassandra as an example
- Include tests validating the tutorial code works with real databases

This would help FastAPI users discover NoSQL options and prove FastAPI's flexibility beyond SQL databases.

### Operating System

macOS

_No response_

### FastAPI Version

0.121.1

### Pydantic Version

2.12.4

### Python Version

3.14.0

### Additional Context

I have prepared [a PR](https://github.com/fastapi/fastapi/pull/14352) with a complete NoSQL tutorial for ScyllaDB/Cassandra, including documentation and code examples.

The tutorial code has been manually tested locally against real ScyllaDB and Cassandra containers using Docker Compose to verify that it works correctly.

**Current testing approach:**
- Automated tests use mocked database operations for fast CI execution without Docker dependencies
- Validates FastAPI structure, routing, and Pydantic models
- Does NOT validate actual database operations in CI

This differs from the SQL tutorial which uses real SQLite (in-memory database).

**Suggested future enhancement:**

- https://awesome-astra.github.io/docs/pages/develop/frameworks/fastapi/

I'm happy to implement integration tests in the initial PR or as a follow-up, depending on maintainer preference.

```python
            model="",

            mcp_servers=[...]
        result = response.json()
```

Synchronization has been set up.

Windows

0.119.1

2.12.3

### Python Version

3.11

### Additional Context

So I created a function to call openAI api as a synchronization request. The length of the message you send the request takes time to respond (for a few seconds). If I run this server as uvicorn and send the request to that function and send the request one more time before the response comes, can server use the method in the next request after the previous response ends?
questions.answer:
As your function is `async` and there is no any `await` inside it, it will be executed in one go without interruption.
So, your worker will only be able to handle 1 request at a time.

If you need to use blocking code in your endpoint functions (like you do in this code example), either convert this endpoint to sync (remove `async` from function signature) or use `run_in_threadpool` to run blocking code inside `async` function.

One more alternative (in your case better use on of the approaches above) is to make `client.beta.messages.create` async and add some `await asyncio.sleep(0)` inside it to let event loop execute other tasks.

### Example Code

```python
import asyncio
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse
import uvicorn

app = FastAPI()

async def event_generator():
    """Generate server-sent events."""
    try:
        count = 0
        while True:
            count += 1
            # SSE format: "data: <message>\n\n"
            yield f"data: Message {count} from server\n\n"
            await asyncio.sleep(1)  # Send a message every second
    finally:
        print("Event generator closed (before await)")
        await asyncio.sleep(0)
        print("Event generator closed (after await)")

@app.get("/sse")
async def sse():
    return StreamingResponse(
        event_generator(),
        media_type="text/event-stream",
        headers={
            "Cache-Control": "no-cache",
            "Connection": "keep-alive",
        }
    )


if __name__ == "__main__":
    uvicorn.run(app, host="0.0.0.0", port=8002)
```


### Description

If I make a call to `/sse` and then cancel it while it's streaming, I expect the code inside finally block to execute. What I'm observing is, it executes until it finds any `await` and then it stalls there. In the above case, I can see the first print in the console but not the second.

Interestingly, it works fine in case of a normal GET API. Sounds like it's something related to asynchronous generator? How should I perform asynchronous cleanups then?

macOS

### Operating System Details

_No response_

### FastAPI Version

0.121.1

### Pydantic Version

2.9.1

### Python Version

3.13.5

_No response_
questions.answer:
`StreamingResponse` is actually just re-imported by FastAPI from Starlette.

And this behavior can be reproduced with Starlette app.
So, this should be reported there: https://github.com/Kludex/starlette

```py
import asyncio

from starlette.applications import Starlette
from starlette.responses import StreamingResponse
from starlette.routing import Route


async def event_generator():
    """Generate server-sent events."""
    try:
        count = 0
        while True:
            count += 1
            yield f"data: Message {count} from server\n\n"
            await asyncio.sleep(1)  # Send a message every second
    finally:
        print("Event generator closed (before await)")
        await asyncio.sleep(0)
        print("Event generator closed (after await)")


def sse(request):
    return StreamingResponse(event_generator(), media_type="text/html")


routes = [
    Route("/sse", sse),
]

app = Starlette(debug=True, routes=routes)

```

questions.question:

### Commit to Help

- [X] I commit to help with one of those options 👆

### Example Code

```python
from fastapi.encoders import jsonable_encoder
from pydantic import RootModel

class Model(RootModel):
    root: int

jsonable_encoder(Model(1))
```


### Description

It seems like jsonable_encoder is mishandling Pydantic's new RootModel. The example raises
"argument of type 'int' is not iterable", caused by this line:

https://github.com/fastapi/fastapi/blob/409e7b503cbac55f0007e4f5f610baaad0da0bcb/fastapi/encoders.py#L241
        if "__root__" in obj_dict:
        
__root__ is no longer used in Pydantic V2

### Operating System

Linux

### Operating System Details

_No response_

### FastAPI Version

0.121.0

### Pydantic Version

2.12.3

### Python Version

3.13.5

### Additional Context

_No response_
questions.answer:
This was a real bug, but it has been fixed upstream. I could reproduce it on FastAPI 0.121.0 (Pydantic 2.12.3), and it no longer occurs from **0.128.0** onwards.

**Cause.** `jsonable_encoder` dumped the model with `model_dump(mode="json")` and then ran a Pydantic v1-era check, `if "__root__" in obj_dict`. In Pydantic v2 a `RootModel` dumps to the bare root value, so for `RootModel[int]` that check became `"__root__" in 1`, which raises `TypeError: argument of type 'int' is not iterable`. It only went unnoticed for list/dict roots because `in` works on them.

The same substring check also broke `RootModel[str]` when the value contained `__root__` (`TypeError: string indices must be integers, not 'str'`).

**Fix.** The `__root__` branch was removed together with Pydantic v1 support in #14609, first released in 0.128.0. I checked the versions directly:

| FastAPI | `jsonable_encoder(Model(1))` |
|---|---|
| 0.121.0 | `TypeError` |
| 0.127.1 | `TypeError` |
| 0.128.0 | `1` |

**If you can't upgrade yet**, unwrap the root yourself: `jsonable_encoder(model.root)` or `model.model_dump(mode="json")`.

Thanks for the clear minimal example. I think this can be closed as fixed.

```python
from fastapi import Request, HTTPException, Depends, APIRouter
from jose import jwt, JWTError

SECRET = "..."
ALGO = "HS256"

def verify_token(request: Request):
    if hasattr(request.state, "user"):  
        return request.state.user
    token = request.cookies.get("access_token")
    if not token:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=401)
    try:
        payload = jwt.decode(token, SECRET, algorithms=[ALGO])
    except JWTError:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=401)
    request.state.user = payload
    return payload

def is_admin(request: Request = Depends(verify_token)):
    user = request.state.user
    if not user.get("is_admin"):
        raise HTTPException(status_code=403)
    return user

root_router = APIRouter(prefix="", dependencies=[Depends(verify_token)])
admin_router = APIRouter(prefix="/admin", dependencies=[Depends(is_admin)])
root_router.include_router(admin_router)
```


### Description

Hi!
Hope you’re doing well.

I’ve got a question regarding how dependencies are executed when using nested APIRouters.

If I attach a dependency like Depends(verify_token) to the root router, I don’t have to repeat token validation in every route — which is great.
However, if I include another router under it (for example /admin) that also defines its own dependency (Depends(is_admin)), both dependencies execute, and the token is validated twice.

This works correctly but feels redundant, since is_admin depends on verify_token anyway.
I’d like to cache the result of the top-level validation so that deeper routers can reuse it instead of triggering another validation pass.

The main step is in     
```
if hasattr(request.state, "user"):  
        return request.state.user
```

The caching workaround with request.state may work fine, but I’m wondering if this approach is recommended at all — or if there’s (or planned) a more native way to reuse the dependency results across routers without re-executing them.

### Operating System

Windows

### Operating System Details

11

### FastAPI Version

0.120.4

### Pydantic Version

v2.11

### Python Version

3.11

### Additional Context

_No response_
questions.answer:
> ```
> ...
> def is_admin(request: Request = Depends(verify_token)):
>     ...
> ```

This will not work. If you annotate parameter with `Request` it's treated as special dependency and you can't use `Depends` with it.

Instead of storing user in `request.state`, you can just return it.
FastAPI has [internal caching mechanism for dependencies](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/dependencies/sub-dependencies/#using-the-same-dependency-multiple-times):

```py
from fastapi import FastAPI, Request, Depends, APIRouter

def verify_token(request: Request):
    print("verify_token called")
    return "payload"

def is_admin(token: str = Depends(verify_token)):
    print("is_admin is called")
    return "user"

root_router = APIRouter(prefix="", dependencies=[Depends(verify_token)])

admin_router = APIRouter(prefix="/admin", dependencies=[Depends(is_admin)])

@admin_router.get("/me")
def read_admin_me(user: str = Depends(is_admin)):
    return {"admin_user": user}


root_router.include_router(admin_router)


app = FastAPI()

app.include_router(router=root_router)
```

Run this and you will see that despite having `verify_token` included 3 times in dependency tree, it will only called once

Either use Pydantic model with `Query` as [described here](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/query-param-models/), or use dataclass with `Depends` as [described here](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/dependencies/classes-as-dependencies/).

> The `Query()` model parameter shows as a **map/object** in Swagger when a `Json[Model]` parameter is present, but shows as **individual query parameters** when the `Json[Model]` parameter is removed.

This (combining query model with other query parameters) is currently not supported.
There is a PR that attempts to add such support: https://github.com/fastapi/fastapi/pull/12481

As for **case 4**, I looked at it only briefly, but it seems to me that the schema is good. Why do you think this is not expected?

In **case 3** the schema is quite general, but I think it can't be improved (as far as I know, there is no way to express such logic for query parameters in openapi)

### Example Code

```python
from types import NoneType
from typing import Iterator, Annotated

from fastapi import APIRouter
from fastapi import Depends
from fastapi import FastAPI


app = FastAPI()


class ApplicationError(Exception): ...


def dependency_with_cleanup_error() -> Iterator[None]:
    yield
    raise ApplicationError()


router = APIRouter(
    dependencies=[Depends(dependency_with_cleanup_error, scope="function")]
)


@router.get("/broken")
def broken():
    # Will return 200, and then fail in the cleanup.
    return {"status": "ok"}


@router.get("/works")
def endpoint(
    v: Annotated[NoneType, Depends(dependency_with_cleanup_error, scope="function")],
):
    # Will correctly return 500
    return {"status": "ok"}


app.include_router(router)
```


### Description

When using the new "scope" feature for yield dependencies, function scope is still cleaned up after the response is sent, if the dependency is requested in the api router, instead of on the path function.

Maybe this is a feature, as in "function" should be interpreted as the scope of where the dependency is requested, and not always the path function, but I can't find any documentation mentioning this behavior, and in any case I'm not sure what the usecase for that would be.

questions.question:

### Commit to Help

- [X] I commit to help with one of those options 👆

### Example Code

```python
from typing import Annotated
from fastapi import FastAPI, Depends, __version__ as fastapi_version
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, BeforeValidator


app = FastAPI()

def comma_separated_str_to_list(value: str) -> list[int]:
    if isinstance(value, str):
        return [int(item) for item in value.split(",") if item.strip().isdigit()]

    if (
        isinstance(value, list)
        and len(value) == 1
        and isinstance(value[0], str)
        and "," in value[0]
    ):
        return comma_separated_str_to_list(value[0])
    
    return value

class ItemSearch(BaseModel):
    id__in: Annotated[Annotated[list[int], BeforeValidator(comma_separated_str_to_list)] | None, Field(alias="item_id_in")] = None

@app.get("/items/")
async def get_items(search: Annotated[ItemSearch, Depends()]):
    return {"search": search, "fastapi_version": fastapi_version}
```


### Description

For legacy reasons, we're using a custom parsing to get list of parameters from a comma separated value with above validator

It was working just fine untile version 0.118.1, but 0.118.2 has changed something (I'm assuming this change #12942) and now the parameter cannot be parsed.

With fastapi 0.118.1:
```bash
$ curl  http://0.0.0.0:8000/items/\?id__in\=1,2,3
{"search":{"id__in":[1,2,3]},"fastapi_version":"0.118.1"}%   
```

With fastapi 0.118.2:
```bash
$ curl  http://0.0.0.0:8000/items/\?id__in\=1,2,3
{"search":{"id__in":null},"fastapi_version":"0.118.2"}%    
```

Side-note, if I remove the alias part, it works fine. Trouble is that in real code it's not that easy to get rid of it
```python
class ItemSearch(BaseModel):
```

questions.title: [BUG] root_path inconsistent behaviour behind a proxy
questions.question:
### First Check

- [X] I added a very descriptive title here.
- [X] I used the GitHub search to find a similar question and didn't find it.
- [X] I searched the FastAPI documentation, with the integrated search.
- [X] I already searched in Google "How to X in FastAPI" and didn't find any information.
- [X] I already read and followed all the tutorial in the docs and didn't find an answer.
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Pydantic](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic).
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Swagger UI](https://github.com/swagger-api/swagger-ui).
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [ReDoc](https://github.com/Redocly/redoc).

### Commit to Help

- [X] I commit to help with one of those options 👆

### Example Code

```python
from typing import Dict
from fastapi import FastAPI, Request
import os

ROOT_PATH = os.getenv("ROOT_PATH", "")


app = FastAPI(
    root_path=ROOT_PATH
)

@app.get("/item")
async def echo(request: Request) -> Dict[str, str]:
    return {
        "path": request.url.path,
        "root_path": request.scope.get("root_path", ""),
    }
```


### Description

In my testing, I found that the command-line option `--root-path` and the FastAPI class argument `root_path` behave very differently. This contradicts the [documentation](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/behind-a-proxy/#setting-the-root-path-in-the-fastapi-app) which states:

> Passing the root_path to FastAPI would be the equivalent of passing the --root-path command line option to Uvicorn or Hypercorn. 

These two options differ even more when combined with proxies either with or without a stripped path prefix.

Below is how the root_path and path variables behave for each combination (using the code I provided above). The FastAPI app is placed behind an `/api` prefix. Each test attempts to reach the desired `/api/item` endpoint:

1. **Stripped path | --root-path** - path: `"/api/item"`, root_path: `"/api"` ✅ Correct
2. **Unstripped path | --root_path** - path: `"/api/api/item"`, root_path: `?` ❌ Endpoint completely unreacheable
3. **Stripped path | root_path argument** - path: `"/item"`, root_path: `"/api"` ⚠️ Endpoint reacheable but path is incorrect *
4. **Unstripped path | root_path argument** - path:`"/api/item"`, root_path:` "/api"` ✅ Correct

As you can see, only two of the four combinations work correctly. Essentially, this means that --root-path should only be used with a stripped path proxy and the fastapi root_path argument should only be used with an unstripped path proxy.

*Option 3 semi-works, however once we try something like redirects, it falls apart. If we request `/api/item/` with a trailing slash, the server will incorrectly redirect us to `/item` (using a 307). In options 1 and 4 the redirects work correctly.

All of this makes working with FastAPI behind a proxy confusing. It would be ideal to unify these options or at least mention this behavior in the documentation. 

(I’m assuming option 2 can’t be fixed directly in FastAPI since the option is passed to Uvicorn. Still, this behavior should probably be at least mentioned in the documentation.)

**I believe this is one of the most common ways FastAPI is deployed, so this bug/uncertainty has the potential to affect a large number of real-world applications.**

⚠️ Note: I only tested this in a Linux Docker container environment. I see no reason why FastAPI would behave differently natively or on Windows, but it’s possible it might work correctly there, or even behave more confusingly.

I should also note that while I’ve found issues addressing parts of this problem in specific scenarios, I haven’t seen a complete demonstration of the full behavior like the one presented here.

### Operating System

Linux

### Operating System Details

Docker container

### FastAPI Version

0.119.1

### Pydantic Version

2.12.3

### Python Version

3.13.2

### Additional Context

Here is a minimal docker setup that I used for this testing:

**/app/main.py** - Already posted above

**Dockerfile**
```
# Build a minimal image for the FastAPI app
FROM python:3.12-slim

ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 \
    PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 \
    PIP_NO_CACHE_DIR=on \
    PIP_DISABLE_PIP_VERSION_CHECK=on

# Install runtime deps
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt /app/
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

# Copy app source
COPY ./app /app

EXPOSE 8000

# Run with proxy headers enabled so uvicorn respects X-Forwarded-*
ENTRYPOINT ["fastapi", "run", "main.py", "--port", "8000", "--proxy-headers", "--forwarded-allow-ips='*'"]

```

**docker-compose.yml**
```
version: "3.9"

services:
  traefik:
    image: traefik:v2.10
    container_name: traefik
    command:
      - --providers.docker=true
      - --providers.docker.exposedbydefault=false
      - --entrypoints.web.address=:80
      - --api.dashboard=true
    ports:
      - "80:80"        # HTTP entrypoint
      - "8080:8080"    # Traefik dashboard
    volumes:
      - /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock:ro
    restart: unless-stopped

  api1:
    build: .
    command: ["--root-path", "/api1"]
    labels:
      - "traefik.enable=true"
      - "traefik.http.routers.api1.rule=PathPrefix(`/api1`)"
      - "traefik.http.routers.api1.entrypoints=web"
      - "traefik.http.services.api1.loadbalancer.server.port=8000"
      - "traefik.http.routers.api1.middlewares=api1-stripprefix,api1-headers"
      - "traefik.http.middlewares.api1-stripprefix.stripprefix.prefixes=/api1"
      - "traefik.http.middlewares.api1-headers.headers.customrequestheaders.X-Forwarded-Prefix=/api"
    depends_on:
      - traefik
    restart: unless-stopped

  api2:
    build: .
    command: ["--root-path", "/api2"]
    labels:
      - "traefik.enable=true"
      - "traefik.http.routers.api2.rule=PathPrefix(`/api2`)"
      - "traefik.http.routers.api2.entrypoints=web"
      - "traefik.http.services.api2.loadbalancer.server.port=8000"
    depends_on:
      - traefik
    restart: unless-stopped

  api3:
    build: .
    environment:
      - ROOT_PATH=/api3
    labels:
      - "traefik.enable=true"
      - "traefik.http.routers.api3.rule=PathPrefix(`/api3`)"
      - "traefik.http.routers.api3.entrypoints=web"
      - "traefik.http.services.api3.loadbalancer.server.port=8000"
      - "traefik.http.routers.api3.middlewares=api3-stripprefix,api3-headers"
      - "traefik.http.middlewares.api3-stripprefix.stripprefix.prefixes=/api3"
      - "traefik.http.middlewares.api3-headers.headers.customrequestheaders.X-Forwarded-Prefix=/api"
    depends_on:
      - traefik
    restart: unless-stopped

  api4:
    build: .
    environment:
      - ROOT_PATH=/api4
    labels:
      - "traefik.enable=true"
      - "traefik.http.routers.api4.rule=PathPrefix(`/api4`)"
      - "traefik.http.routers.api4.entrypoints=web"
      - "traefik.http.services.api4.loadbalancer.server.port=8000"
    depends_on:
      - traefik
    restart: unless-stopped

networks:
  default:
    name: fastapi-proxy-demo

```
questions.answer:
Thanks for flagging this!

The inconsistency between root_path and --root-path is definitely problematic. I don't want to unnecessarily provide two ways of achieving the same thing, when there's a canonical standard way to do it. So I'm now deprecating the parameter `root_path` from `FastAPI` in favor of the command flags and the ASGI provided ones.

The parameter root_path was there as a way to achieve what the old openapi_prefix did in a way closer to the ASGI standard, it was before Uvicorn provided a way to configure it (or before I realized it was there that it should be configured).

But it's always been there bothering me, so now I went ahead and deprecated it.

questions.question:
### First Check

### Commit to Help

- [X] I commit to help with one of those options 👆

### Example Code

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI

app = FastAPI()

@app.get("/A/B/{param}")
async def get_param{param: str):
    return {"param": param}
```


### Description

I am currently working on a FastAPI application and are standardizing URL handling for consistency.
The goal is for all routes:

are case-insensitive (e.g. /A/B == /a/b)

are trailing-slash-insensitive (e.g. /path == /path/)

and that path parameters remain untouched (e.g. /A/B/{param} preserves BLABLA<<uppercase>> exactly as sent)

I have already implemented this behavior successfully using an ASGI middleware that normalizes scope["path"] before routing.

However, I feel that we could implement this more natively by extending or overriding the compile_path() function in Starlette’s routing layer.


What I did test 


I tried a CustomRoute approach by subclassing APIRoute and modifying matches() or get_route_handler(), but:

matches() runs after the router starts path matching.

Changes to scope["path"] inside that method are local and not persistent across routes.

The router continues using the original case-sensitive regex generated by compile_path().

I then examined the Starlette compile_path() implementation and noticed that route regexes are built with exact casing and strict slash matching.

This means that if we could make compile_path() emit case-insensitive regexes (for example by prefixing with (?i) or allowing optional trailing /), the behavior would be consistent across all routes without needing middleware



### Operating System

Linux

### Operating System Details

_No response_

0.112.2

### Pydantic Version

2.8.2

### Python Version

3.11

_No response_
questions.answer:
If your need is to allow this on the client side, it’s purely a URL-rewriting task that fits middleware perfectly.
If you need to standardize internal path definitions, you should also act at the routing level and ensure a consistent convention is enforced.

questions.title: Regression in 0.118.2: BeforeValidator not called for query parameters with Annotated types
questions.question:
### First Check

- [X] I added a very descriptive title here.
- [X] I used the GitHub search to find a similar question and didn't find it.
- [X] I searched the FastAPI documentation, with the integrated search.
- [X] I already searched in Google "How to X in FastAPI" and didn't find any information.
- [X] I already read and followed all the tutorial in the docs and didn't find an answer.
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Pydantic](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic).
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Swagger UI](https://github.com/swagger-api/swagger-ui).
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [ReDoc](https://github.com/Redocly/redoc).

### Commit to Help

- [X] I commit to help with one of those options 👆

### Example Code

```python
"""Demonstrates BeforeValidator regression in FastAPI 0.118.2"""
import dataclasses
from typing import Annotated, Optional
from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BeforeValidator, PlainSerializer
from starlette.testclient import TestClient


# Custom class (similar to MongoDB ObjectId, Version objects, etc.)
@dataclasses.dataclass(frozen=True)
class StudyVersion:
    """Represents a study version like '8.8' or '880'"""
    major: int
    minor: int
    patch: int = 0

    @classmethod
    def parse(cls, value):
        if value is None:
            return None
        if isinstance(value, StudyVersion):
            return value
        # Parse "8.8" format
        if isinstance(value, str) and "." in value:
            parts = value.split(".")
            return cls(int(parts[0]), int(parts[1]) if len(parts) > 1 else 0)
        # Parse 880 -> (8, 8, 0)
        value_int = int(value)
        return cls(value_int // 100, (value_int % 100) // 10, value_int % 10)

    def __str__(self):
        return f"{self.major}.{self.minor}" if self.minor else f"{self.major}"


# Type definition (common pattern in production code)
StudyVersionStr = Annotated[
    StudyVersion,
    BeforeValidator(StudyVersion.parse),
    PlainSerializer(str)
]

app = FastAPI()


@app.post("/studies", response_model=None)
def create_study(name: str, version: Optional[StudyVersionStr] = None):
    """
    In 0.118.1: version is correctly parsed to StudyVersion instance
    In 0.118.2: version stays None, BeforeValidator is not called
    """
    print(f"version parameter: {version!r}")
    return {
        "name": name,
        "version": str(version) if version else None,
    }


if __name__ == "__main__":
    import fastapi
    print(f"Testing with FastAPI {fastapi.__version__}")

    client = TestClient(app)
    response = client.post("/studies?name=test&version=8.8")
    print(f"Response: {response.json()}")

    # Expected in 0.118.1:
    #   version parameter: StudyVersion(major=8, minor=8, patch=0)
    #   Response: {'name': 'test', 'version': '8.8'}  ✅

    # Actual in 0.118.2:
    #   version parameter: None
    #   Response: {'name': 'test', 'version': None}  ❌
```


### Description

## Description

  In FastAPI **0.118.1**, `BeforeValidator` works correctly with `Optional[Annotated[T, BeforeValidator(...)]]` query parameters:
  - Query parameter `?version=8.8` is parsed to `StudyVersion(major=8, minor=8, patch=0)` ✅
  - The validator function is called as expected

  In FastAPI **0.118.2**, the same code **silently breaks**:
  - Query parameter `?version=8.8` is ignored, endpoint receives `version=None` ❌
  - `BeforeValidator` is **not called at all**
  - No error raised at startup, validation is completely bypassed

  ### Root cause

  This regression appears to be introduced by **PR #12942** ("Fix tagged discriminated union not recognized as body field").

  While the PR correctly fixes discriminated unions, it inadvertently breaks `BeforeValidator` execution for query parameters with `Annotated` types.

  ### Impact

  This is a **silent regression** affecting production code:
  - Custom version objects (e.g., StudyVersion)
  - Custom ID types with parsing logic
  - Any domain-specific value objects using `BeforeValidator`

  The application starts without errors, but validation logic is completely bypassed and endpoints receive `None` instead of validated objects.


### Operating System

Linux

### Operating System Details

_No response_

### FastAPI Version

0.118.2

### Pydantic Version

2.12.0

### Python Version

3.11.13

### Additional Context

_No response_
questions.answer:
Since your actual type (`StudyVersion`) is complex, FastAPI treats it as `Body` parameter, but you send it as `Query`, that's why it's `None`.
For me it's more strange that it worked before 0.118.2. 

So, it looks like it worked because of the bug, and that bug was fixed by https://github.com/fastapi/fastapi/pull/12942.

For simple types it works as expected:
```py
from typing import Annotated, Optional
from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BeforeValidator
from starlette.testclient import TestClient

MyAnnotatedType = Annotated[str, BeforeValidator(lambda x: f"p_{x}")]

app = FastAPI()

@app.post("/")
def post_(param: Optional[MyAnnotatedType] = None):
    return {"param": param}

def test_():
    client = TestClient(app)
    response = client.post("/", params={"param": "value"})
    assert response.status_code == 200, response.text
    assert response.json() == {"param": "p_value"}
```

questions.answer:
### Fix

 Your happy-path test is the only one that needs startup state. Since `TestClient(app)` is created without a context manager, the lifespan startup does not run, templates are not loaded, and your handler likely returns 404 for “template not found.” Use a context-managed client so startup runs, and align your model keys.

---

#### Minimal fix: run lifespan in tests

```python
# conftest.py or test_main.py
import pytest
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient
from app.main import app

@pytest.fixture(scope="module")
def client():
    # This triggers lifespan startup and shutdown
    with TestClient(app) as c:
        yield c
```

Update tests to use the fixture:

```python
def test_valid_method(client, good_test):
    resp = client.post("/template1/", json=good_test)
    assert resp.status_code == 200
    assert resp.headers["Content-Type"] == "application/json"
```

---

#### Make the failure obvious

```python
def test_root(client):
    r = client.get("/")
    data = r.json()
    assert r.status_code == 200
    # Ensure templates actually loaded during tests
    assert len(data.get("loaded_templates", [])) > 0
```

---

#### Key gotchas to clean up

* **Model vs payload keys**
  Your model shows `table: List[Table1]` but tests send `table1`. Your route also checks `payload.table1`. Pick one name and use it everywhere. Example:

  ```python
  class Template1Payload(BaseModel):
      docId: str
      salutation: str
      firstName: str
      familyName: str
      table1: list[Table1]   # align with tests
  ```

  And in the handler:

  ```python
  if not payload.table1:
      raise HTTPException(status_code=400, detail="Table 1 missing")
  ```

* **Correct runner guard**
  In `main.py` change

  ```python
  if name == "main":
  ```

  to

  ```python
  if __name__ == "__main__":
      import uvicorn
      uvicorn.run(app, host="127.0.0.1", port=80, log_level="info")
  ```

* **Trailing slash**
  You mounted `router = APIRouter(prefix="/template1")` and `@router.post("/")`.
  Your test uses `"/template1/"`, which is correct. Keep them consistent.

---

#### Optional: speed up unit tests with mocks

```python
from unittest.mock import patch

@patch("app.templates.get_all", return_value={"template1": "<html>...</html>"})
@patch("app.pdf.generate_pdf", return_value=b"%PDF-1.4 ...")
def test_valid_method(mock_pdf, mock_templates, client, good_test):
    r = client.post("/template1/", json=good_test)
    assert r.status_code == 200
```

---

#### Why other tests pass

* Missing or bad payloads fail at Pydantic validation or your early checks, so they never touch the template store.
* Only the happy path needs loaded templates, which are empty if startup never ran, so you get a 404.
